attributes.description:
This dataset contains emails sent by community members and staff to the City Council Hotline as well as staff and council responses to those emails.

Note: All emails to hotlineopendata@bouldercolorado.gov are public record. Email addresses and phone numbers are automatically hashed with a long alphanumeric string in the data for privacy reasons. Visit https://bouldercolorado.gov/boulder-city-council-hotline for more information on contacting the City Council Hotline.

Dear Councilmembers: As part of the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan major update, the team is planning to convene a Process Subcommittee. This group will consist of City and County staff and one member from each of the four approval bodies: City of Boulder Planning Board, Boulder City Council, Boulder County Planning Commission, and Board of County Commissioners. Council is being asked to identify one member to be on this Subcommitee, which will be presented for your consideration as a Matters Item on Thursday, November 7. The purpose of the Process Subcommittee is to discuss and confirm the process elements for conducting the update to the Comprehensive Plan, on matters such as the community engagement schedule, policy analysis timelines, and the final approval process mechanics. As the name implies, the subcommittee will not review, discuss, or provide any guidance on the content of the plan, but only focus on the process itself. We envision the subcommittee meeting only three or four times throughout the entire update, with the first meeting occurring before the end of 2024. Please contact me with any questions. Kind regards, Brad Mueller, AICP Director, Planning & Development Services Department City of Boulder

Mayor, Mayor Pro Tem and Council Members - I want to make you aware of a communication I have just sent to community member Andrew O???Connor in reference to a request he made that the city remove flyers he found objectionable from the round billboards on the Pearl Street Mall. While operations staff with Parks and Recreation did remove the flyers referenced by Mr. O???Connor, as well as other materials related to the conflict in the Middle East, I needed to clarify that despite what I believe were staff's good intentions, such removal was done too hastily. As a city, we are committed to upholding the First Amendment. As such, we cannot make content-based decisions about what is displayed in these public locations. As you can see from the email contents below, the city will be shoring up its policies and practices to prevent this from happening again. At the same time, it was important for me as city manager and as an individual who is deeply committed to equity and inclusivity to use my voice to condemn historically inaccurate and harmful statements made by Mr. O???Connor, both in his original request and in follow-up communication with Council Member Mark Wallach. For full transparency with other council members, the message sent directly to Council Member Wallach included statements denying the Holocaust occurred and minimizing the devastating atrocities that occurred during that time. I am truly sorry for the understandable distress the statements made by Mr. O???Connor and the resulting staff action has caused. This is a challenging time for our community, made more so by this type of ugly discourse, and I reiterate that the City of Boulder will not tolerate discrimination or violence against any group of individuals based on their faith or personal identity. Regards, Nuria For full transparency, the following is the correspondence I sent to Mr. O???Connor: Dear Andrew, I am writing to you as city manager to address your recent request that the city remove flyers that were posted on Pearl Street Mall in relation to the events that occurred in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. As you have been informed, the round billboards on the Mall are managed by our Parks and Recreation Department. After receiving your email request, operations staff with Parks and Recreation made the decision to remove all content related to the conflict in the Middle East, including the flyers you referenced. While I believe staff acted in good faith, they were unfortunately too hasty in removing such flyers. Political speech is protected by our Constitution, and if we as a local government are going to provide a ???town square??? opportunity for paper materials to be posted in a city park, we cannot make content-based decisions. While we cannot undo the removal of this material, I want to be very clear that the city will be strengthening its policies and practices to guide how these billboards are managed in the future. We will be working closely with our City Attorney???s Office to ensure that our First Amendment obligations are considered in these policies, and future requests that you may make regarding what you consider to be objectionable content will be handled differently. On behalf of the city organization and speaking for myself, I also want to make clear that we disagree with your conclusions that the flyers depicting pictures of Israelis missing after Oct. 7 constitute ???false propaganda??? or is akin to ???hate speech.??? I also cannot stand by silently in response to additional correspondence you have had with Council Member Mark Wallach in which you deny that the Holocaust happened. While I will defend your right to free speech, this kind of harmful and historically inaccurate content is not consistent with our city values and is not conducive to a meaningful dialogue around the complex issues in the Middle East. The City of Boulder will not tolerate discrimination or violence against any group of individuals based on their faith or personal identity. Regards, Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde City Manager (pronouns: she/her/ella) What's This? EMPLOYERS WHO ARE MOST IMPACTED: I???m trying to understand the scale of employers who are likely to be significantly impacted by the expenses of a higher minimum wage relative to their net income (or otherwise their ability to withstand it). As the easiest way I can think of to try and quantify this, can you say approximately how many small businesses Boulder has (i.e., fewer than 25 employees, which I understand represents 81% of Boulder???s 8,400 business overall) who are also employers of minimum wage employees? I???d also welcome other ways to think about the idea of which employers are expected to be most significantly impacted and the scale of that impact. #2. EMPLOYERS WHO IMPLEMENT CITY BUSINESS: Now I'm thinking about employers who are carrying out the mission of the city and working on the public's behalf. The question: What is the number of employers who are contractors or grantees of the city that rely on minimum wage workers???and can you categorize them by what they do somehow? Thanks so much! [Sending on behalf of Chandler and Marcy due to technology challenges.] ------------ Dear Council, Thank you, Mayor Pro-Tem Folkerts and Councilmember Winer for your questions about the Planning Board????????s recommended motion that Council consider revoking the landmark designation of the Silver Saddle buildings at 90 Arapahoe Ave. Here is information on the current state of buildings, Inclusionary Housing units in landmarked properties, and the process for this evening????????s decision and the general process for revoking a landmark designation. Staff will be available this evening to answer additional questions. In short, Council cannot remove a landmark designation without going through the process as outlined in the B.R.C. section 9-11-10. Should council wish to remove the requirement to pursue landmarking from the Annexation Agreement, please provide that direction tonight and continue the item to a future meeting and give staff direction to incorporate such amendments which will then be brought back for consideration on the Consent Agenda. Current State of Buildings The project at 90 Arapahoe is paused mid-construction. City Council designated a portion of the property as an individual landmark in 2021, and the Landmarks Board approved a Landmark Alteration Certificate to rehabilitate the buildings and construct additions. The approval included restoration OR in-kind replacement of log siding if, during construction, it was determined to be beyond repair. The approval also included replacement of the roof and most windows and enclosure of the carports. In their review, the Landmarks Board found that the changes were consistent with the historic preservation criteria and guidelines. In general, Section 9-11-20 Property Maintenance Required of the Boulder Revised Code requires designated properties to be maintained at a minimum in the condition they were at the time of designation. Temporary removal of historic materials may occur during rehabilitation if within the scope of the approved LAC. However, removal of materials may not be used as a reason to justify revocation of a landmark designation. Process and Criteria to Revoke Landmark Designation Status The process to revoke the landmark designation of a property is outlined in Section 9-11-10 Revocation of Designation, B.R.C. 1981, which provides that if a designated building is lawfully relocated or demolished, the owner may apply to the Landmarks Board to revoke the designation. An application to revoke a designation may also start from Council or the Landmarks Board, or a recognized historic preservation organization. The process is the same as the designation process: Public hearing on revocation before Landmarks Board (LB) Public hearing before City Council (if revocation is recommended by LB) or call up by City Council of disapproval of revocation by LB (if City Council chooses to call it up). The Landmarks Board and Council would need to determine that the property no longer meets the purposes and standards of sections???????9-11-1, "Legislative Intent," and???????9-11-2, "City Council May Designate or Amend Landmarks and Historic Districts," B.R.C. 1981. Inclusionary Housing in Historic Buildings One of the city????????s Inclusionary Housing units is located a few blocks east in a small stone cottage that is individually landmarked. It was fully renovated and placed on the market in 2016. The number of applicants for the unit was two to three times higher than the average at that time, indicating there may be strong interest in IH homes with historic character. The IH program recognizes that all units require maintenance and require an education class for new owners. The program also recognizes homes over 20 years old may take more to maintain. The Capital Improvement Policy was updated in the last few years to allow additional investment in older homes. The credit is $30,000 for homes up to 20 years old, and $50,000 for homes over 20 years old and for homeowners who have owned the property for more than 15 years. Owners of individually landmarked properties are eligible for a State Historic Preservation Tax Credit to help off-set the cost of rehabilitation. The maximum credit in general is $100,000 and is equal to 20% of the qualifying costs. Since the CIP policy caps investment at $50,000, the maximum credit for owners of Inclusionary Housing units is $10,000. The credit resets every 10 years or upon the sale of the property. For projects that are part of a larger redevelopment project, the historic buildings are completely renovated before they enter the IH program. For the stone cottage mentioned above, the renovation included a new roof structure, stabilizing the exterior walls, a new foundation, and new windows and doors. In the last nine years, two Landmark Alteration Certificates have been reviewed and approved to repoint the masonry and install solar panels. Existing Proposed Motion for Consent Agenda Item 3D Staff did not advance the Planning Board recommendation to remove the landmark designation in the Council memo and draft motion for approval, recognizing that Planning Board did not have all of this additional information at the time of its decision. After additional consultation with Historic Preservation staff, the following considerations informed this decision: The buildings will be fully renovated, providing the owners with buildings in a condition comparable to new construction. The Inclusionary Housing unit at 210 Arapahoe Avenue (an individual landmark) had two to three times the average number of applicants. Inclusionary Housing units in designated properties provide unique architectural character in established neighborhoods that may be highly desirable to a number of applicants. The approved Landmark Alteration Certificate (HIS2018-00069) and Building Permits (BLD-SFA2022-00044 and BLD-SFA2022-00045 stated that the wood siding would be assessed and if rotted, replaced in-kind. Staff considers the project to be mid-construction, and that the approved rehabilitation will preserve the historic integrity of the buildings. Additionally, the property owner is responsible for repairs or maintenance necessary to prevent significant deterioration of the exterior of the buildings beyond their condition at the time of designation. Please note that this item involves consideration of amendments to the annexation agreement. If council was interested in allowing for consideration of removal or amendment of the existing landmark designations for buildings, staff would recommend that council pull the item off of the Consent Agenda, to approve an additional amendment to the annexation agreement that would remove the requirement to pursue landmarking of those buildings. As noted above, removal or amendment of an existing designation requires a separate quasi-judicial process (criteria-based, unbiased analysis and decision) that would involve both the Landmarks Board and City Council. Such process could be pursued in the future if the requirement to pursue designation was removed from the annexation agreement. We look forward to answering any additional questions, should you have them this evening. Thank you, Marcy Gerwing, Principal Historic Preservation Planner Chandler Van Schaack, Principal Development Review Planner ------------------------------------- Brad Mueller, AICP Director (pronouns: he/him/his) O [5d8d54d2c868dbd723feed1c11a8091a67f9a62c6288b2e6054a9d8d0b542bbf] [e64ca61455f44dd2a0e2511e9fce5ac55188ae0f7c1d339a034cbe763aa8c60d] Planning & Development Services Department 1739 Broadway | Boulder, CO 80302 bouldercolorado.gov

A new Council term and a new Hotline! What could be better? (Don????????t answer that.) In any event, I have a number of questions to raise and comments to make with respect to the poll on community preferences, the conclusions drawn from it, and the staff recommendations. My comments fall into two major areas: housing and transportation. Housing: 1) Apparently most respondents would like to see more affordable housing. I am astonished! The real issue is how to produce it. Without firm affordability requirements the private market will continue to produce expensive market-rate rentals and uber-expensive housing for sale. We need to create more affordable housing units that are suitable for families to purchase and develop a specific gameplan for doing so. 2) Again, the ???????commitments to increasing the housing supply???????? and ???????increasing diversity of housing types across the city???????? will not provide the intended results unless steps are taken to insure the affordability of that housing. Townhouses in Boulder typically sell for $1.5MM and up. It is not housing typology that counts, it is price. 3) While there is broad support for creating more housing, it appears that not one of Boulder????????s neighborhoods generated more than 31% support as a desirable location to build it. Apparently poll respondents were in full support of building more housing - but somewhere else. 4) Responses to the poll are occasionally inconsistent. Limiting additional housing types to transit-related areas, and permitting them throughout residential areas both received majority support. Responses to the development of Area III are all over the map. Investment in supportive housing is key because housing ends homelessness, plain and simple. Engagement and sheltering are only effective if there are resources to provide to people. Another day, another Hotline??? At this week???s meeting of the City Council we will be considering ??? and almost certainly passing ??? Ordinance 8585, an act that will increase occupancy limits to a maximum of 5 unrelated individuals in a unit of housing, up from the current limit of 3 or 4, depending upon where the property is located. I have previously expressed my opposition to the proposed ordinance and wish to offer some last thoughts as to the basis of that opposition. For the sake of brevity (as defined by my rather loose standards), I will limit my comments to the following two issues: The first is the elephant in the room: In 2021 the voters of Boulder declined to approve the Bedrooms Are For People initiative, which would have provided for an occupancy increase equal to the number of bedrooms in the residence, plus one. That initiative was rejected by approximately 53% of the voters. How is that decision to be treated by a Council majority desirous of increasing Boulder???s occupancy limits? I contend that a clear, specific vote by the community on a matter such as this should supersede the desires of a Council majority to move in the opposite direction. The voting results of initiatives are not merely suggestions to Council; they are instructions directing Council how to proceed. In this case there was nothing vague or subtle about those instructions. We were directed to maintain the then-existing occupancy limits; no other interpretation is viable. It has been suggested that the proposed ordinance does not conflict with the results of the 2021 vote because in the new ordinance the permitted increase in occupancy is a flat figure (five) and is not based on the number of bedrooms in a residence. This is fiction worthy of a Pulitzer Prize: does anyone really believe that the voters in 2021 would have risen up and rallied to the banner of increased occupancy if only we had changed the manner in which occupancy limits were calculated? The proposition does not even pass the test of common sense. The real difference between then and now is that in one instance thousands of voters ??? aka, the electorate - rendered a clear verdict on this subject; in this instance the majority of a group of nine will ignore that verdict (or deny that it was a verdict at all) and impose its own standard, one that is even more draconian than that which was rejected at the polls. This is the elevation of the will of the Council majority over the expressed will of the community as a whole. It is the negation of a legitimate vote taken by the community of Boulder. A more valid response to the 2021 result would be to return this decision to the voters to determine if they have had a change of heart. Perhaps they have; you never know. Instead, the decision of the people of Boulder in 2021 will simply be overridden and nullified by several members of this Council. Haven???t we seen this movie before? Why should it be more justifiable at the local level than it is nationally? The merits of increased occupancy limits are entirely irrelevant to this conversation, as is the wisdom of the community in voting down such increases. Maybe the voters erred in doing so, but it is not this Council???s place to decide that and ???fix??? their mistake. Overturning an election result is a violation of core democratic principles and should have been regarded by this body as an inappropriate use of its authority. Elections do ??? or are supposed to ??? matter, even in today???s climate. We work for the people; when we disrespect their decision and simply impose our own we act as if the reverse was true. The second basis of my opposition is the perplexing unwillingness of my colleagues to provide any type of protection or relief for the University-adjacent communities. The problem is simple: some of our neighborhoods will disproportionately bear the brunt of the effects of the proposed ordinance. This Council has been asked by a plethora of residents in these neighborhoods for relief from the impact of this ordinance. To date the Council majority has been unresponsive to these requests. Sound governance requires a spirit of compromise and nuance, both of which are absent here. There has been little discussion as to why we cannot accommodate ??? or even attempt to accommodate - these neighborhood requests. Different situations should be treated differently, but this Council shows no inclination to respond to the specific needs of these communities. And although I said I would discuss only two issues, I have to at least briefly note that the new ordinance does not make even the most feeble gesture at ensuring affordability for the new, additional tenants. Ordinance 8585 is, instead, nothing more than a real estate investor???s dream. It is an inconvenient truth that in 2021 the community rejected a change to our current occupancy limits; at this week???s meeting this Council will reject the judgement of the community. The anger, frustration, and sense of disenfranchisement that this course of action has generated among so many should be no surprise to this body or any of its members. You vote, you win, but if Council dislikes the outcome you lose: is this how we do it now? Welcome to Boulder.

Is this correct or not? 3) Do we anticipate that the 20-year term limit on agreements will inhibit our ability to enter into P3 relationships? Will we need to do 30-year agreements? 4) In the memo it is noted that Fire Stations 2 and 4 will be designed after the land for those facilities is acquired. Have we put any limitation on the expense of those facilities, so that we can design towards that limitation, and value engineer the structures if necessary to meet that goal? Leaving the process open-ended is how we end up with a $35MM fire station, such as the one presently under construction. Designing first and budgeting second is precisely the reverse order in which we should proceed. 5) The memo speaks of 3% (preferably 4%) of current replacement value (CRV) be set aside each year towards the upkeep of the structures. Can anyone estimate what this figure will look like on an annual basis if the entire program of the Facilities Master Plan is implemented? And these funds will be found where? I fully support the goal (I believe strongly in the proper maintenance of our capital assets), but question our ability to carry this out. Please provide reassurance.

Apparently in direct response to my Hotline post of yesterday (at least, that is my theory), Congress has roused itself from its stupor and passed a funding bill, thus avoiding a government shutdown. I therefore withdraw my request for CAC to schedule a report from the City Manager at the October 5 meeting as to how such a shutdown would impact Boulder, and the manner in which we would deal with such impacts.

As an initial matter, I am amazed that our staff, having provided such a weak justification for conveying rather than leasing our library properties to the Library District, is turning to counsel for the Library District to make the case for them. As the Library District has been approved by the voters it is necessary to negotiate an Intergovernmental Agreement between the parties; that is certainly not in dispute. Nor is it in dispute that we need to do so in a way that permits them to operate effectively and carry out their mission. However, there still remain interests of the City that should be protected in this process, and I am hard-pressed to identify any of those interests that staff has actually sought to protect. If staff is not going to do so there is no need to actually negotiate the IGA; we should simply get a list of what the Library District wants and put it in the document. A negotiation does not require the parties to be adversaries, as we are not in this case. But we ought to at least have some advocacy for matters of significance to the City. The first key question is whether the physical assets of our libraries (as opposed to the books) should be leased to the District or conveyed. I must ask: what community outreach has been done on such a consequential decision? If we have not done so, why not? Do we not believe that the public might want to express themselves on this matter? The memo prepared by counsel for the District (the ???District Memo???), argues for conveyance of these assets. The claim is that ownership is necessary for the District to raise even more money through the sale or pledge of these assets. It then goes deep in the weeds of financing options to explain the benefits of conveyance over leasing, but I will try to unpack it to the best of my ability. The District Memo states that they would never issue bonds, and if they did they would never constitute a claim against the physical assets of the library system. Is their position that they would never issue bonds because there are better financing vehicles (discussed below) or because they cannot? I think the answer is the former, which makes non-issuance of bonds an act of forbearance, not limitation. Instead, the District Memo lays out their preferred method of financing: a sale-leaseback transaction in which we effectively sell the properties to a third party in exchange for a loan, which is paid back by the District through lease payments, which are, in turn, funded by tax revenues. Is this not a conveyance of the property to a third party, subject to the District???s ability to maintain title if it makes all of its payments? This is precisely what some of us fear: exposing these assets to foreclosure if the payments are not made. I note that the District Memo does not state that Certificate of Participation financing does not create an interest in our properties by a third-party lender; it merely implies that this would never be a problem because they say it would never be a problem. Despite the fact that the District is being funded at a service level higher than any department in City government, basically the ???vision??? level of funding, they appear to have just realized that part of their responsibilities includes properly maintaining their assets, and they appear to believe that the sums of money they will receive from the taxpayers should be net of the cost of those maintenance obligations. I am not sure that the community would view it that way. But if the District is concerned with the cost of those repairs, I would like to suggest an alternative method of financing those repairs that would be consistent with leasing the properties: a revolving fund from the City, say $5MM (although the amount could certainly be discussed), which could be drawn down as needed by the District and used for maintenance and repairs, and repaid by the District at reasonable -or even favorable- interest rates, and reusable as the fund is repaid. I would rather the City be the lender to the District, than a hedge fund or investor group through Certificate of Participation financing. As far as the claim that generational planning is impinged upon by a 20-year lease term, this is just silly. This relationship is permanent, as determined by the voters; there is simply no possibility that any lease would not be renewed at the end of its term. However, if legally permitted I would be prepared to include a 20-year renewal option in the lease; and if that is not permitted, I believe that under certain circumstances the Charter permits a 30-year term. But I do want to point out that we have a number of lease relationships with entities such as the Dairy, who seem to overcome this hardship without undue difficulty. The idea that we would not renew the lease, and that generational planning is thereby constrained, is not substantive. There is simply too much nonsense being promulgated in this discussion, and not enough common sense. I still have not heard a compelling argument for transferring these assets, owned and paid for by the City, when all of the goals of the District can be met via a lease transaction. I wish that staff had actually represented the concerns raised above in these negotiations, so that I could spend less time writing Hotlines and more time watching football.

As I have been entirely dilatory in preparing this Hotline (the influence of spring weather?), these comments represent my thoughts on the zoning topic we will be addressing on Thursday; I do not expect any sort of response to them from staff on such egregiously short notice. I first want to acknowledge the work put in by staff in making these proposals to us, and the thought that has gone into them ??? even when I disagree with their conclusions. But this is clearly a considered document that is responsive to the issues raised by Council. Nevertheless, I have the following comments: 1) The proposal to reduce lot size in RL-1 zones from 7,000sf to 4,000 sf comes without any explanation as to why, and what the tangible benefits will be from doing so. What is it? If it is that this will permit the development of more affordable homes and/or duplexes, has anyone studied what it would cost to acquire such a lot and either construct a small home on it or, alternatively, two duplex units? I have no objection to small homes or duplexes, but if the goal is to create ???attainable??? or ???missing middle??? housing (names that are essentially without definition and are used rather indiscriminately in the conversation about how to create more affordable housing), should we not at least analyze if the actions we are taking are at all related to the goal we are hoping to achieve? Has anyone looked at the numbers? For example: if a 7,000 sf lot costs $800,000, perhaps a 4,000 sf lot will be purchasable for $400,000. At $400 per square foot (or more) to construct a new 2,000 square foot home, that is another $800,000. Throw in architects, brokers, fees and profit and voila!: you have just built a $1.5MM home. With respect to affordability, I can only say: big deal; why did we bother? Is the shortage of $1.5MM homes the housing crisis we mean to address? 2) Likewise, the proposals for the RR zones will not achieve anything of value for this community. These proposals by and large adhere to the concept that building more housing will create more affordable housing. This is simply untrue, at least in Boulder. If a developer buys a home on a 20,000 sf lot with the intent of selling 2 houses, and purchases the property for $1.45MM (our current median price, and unlikely for such a sizeable property), and builds a new house of 2,500 sf (also on the small side for what will be a 10,000 sf lot) at $400 per square foot, that developer is now into the project for $2.45MM, before factoring in fees, architecture, brokerage and profit. If he wants to refurbish the existing house (assume that one is also 2,500 sf) and spends $150 per square foot to do so, that is another $375,000 he would need to recover. In short, this project will create 2 houses that need to collectively sell for a total of $3MM (or more), or $1.5MM each. If he builds larger or fancier houses, we could be looking at $1.75MM-$2.5MM for each house. Exactly what have we achieved in doing this? What is the social benefit in doing so? What is the purpose of such high-end density? Without some requirement of affordability, this is nothing more than an opportunity for developers to make more money on their projects; the people of Boulder will receive nothing of value for this density. 3) I remain perplexed at the concept of ???missing middle??? housing and the notion that it should somehow be exempt from ordinary approval processes. Is this the same as the term ???attainable ??? housing that was the nomenclature du jour a while back? Would ???missing middle??? include the new proposal for 300 square foot efficiency units that has been reported will rent for $2,500 per month? On a per square foot basis, these units will be among the most expensive ??? if not THE most expensive ??? units in Boulder, at $100 per square foot per year. That would be the equivalent of renting a 700 square foot one- bedroom apartment for over $5,800/month. What about a $7,000/month townhome? Does that warrant exemption from use review? Again, if there is no affordability attached to these projects, there is no principled basis for favorable treatment during review. 4) With respect to incentivizing the conversion to residential of industrial properties, I think there is some merit there, but we should remain protective of the service industrial properties we all rely upon. I do not relish the prospect of driving to Longmont for a shoe repair, but that is the direction in which we are headed. 5) In summary, we cannot operate on the presumption that there is a social benefit to density because it will lead to such an abundance of housing that developers will slash their expenses to levels affordable to our in-commuters and first responders. That may be the case if there is an excess supply of potatoes in the market, but that is not how it works in real estate and that is not how it works in any major housing market of which I am aware. What is lacking in this analysis is the nexus between increasing Boulder???s density and the creation of more affordable housing. We all agree on the goal: Boulder is desperate for housing that is affordable to people who are not living off of trust funds or are tech entrepreneurs. But density itself is not a strategy to get us there; it is simply a form of magical thinking that sounds good, feels good, but lacks substance.

As I will not be present for Thursday????????s discussion of inclusionary housing fees on demolitions and major renovations ( I am in NY, experiencing a combination of terrible weather and mediocre theater), I thought I would offer a few thoughts on the subject: 1) The staff memo notes that ???????in the absence of interventions available land is often developed with large expensive housing, which both reduces opportunities for more affordable housing and contributes to a general rise in prices for all housing in the community.???????? I suggest that no such interventions will be effective in an environment where vacant lots of 6,000 sf trade for $700K and up, and the smallest homes sell for over $1MM. A $25-45K fee will not deter the development of large expensive housing, because you cannot feasibly construct smaller, less expensive housing in light of the cost to acquire the land, demolish the existing house and construct a new one. 2) As I read the staff memo, there appear to be 2 rationales for imposing an inclusionary housing fee on demolitions/new construction: The first is to raise money for affordable housing. This will certainly occur. The Nexus study suggests that we will receive annual revenues of $1.25MM from inclusionary housing fees (I do not recall seeing a breakout of what portion of the funds that would be received is allocable to major alterations). I would be happy to have Boulder receive these funds, although the amounts that will be raised will hardly be transformational. 3) The implied second rational is that this program will serve as an intervention to alter behavior, making extremely large homes less attractive to construct, resulting in smaller, more affordable housing. This will certainly not occur. Those who are building 5,000-6,000 square foot houses can easily afford the fee (although they will not like it). For a teardown of a 1,000 sf house to be replaced by a 5,000 sf house, the fee would be based on the additional square footage of 4,000 sf. At $15 per square foot the fee would be $60,000. However, at a construction cost of, say, $700 per square foot, a reduction in square footage of only 100 square feet ???????? or 2% of a 5,000 square foot structure - would reduce the construction cost by $70,000, essentially keeping the cost of development the same as without the fee. No fee supportable by the nexus study will alter behaviors in the construction of large homes. 4) With respect to substantial additions, we have defined them as costing $250,000 and adding at least 500 square feet of floor area. My first question: why do we need to meet both criteria? Years ago, I built a house in the Chautauqua neighborhood. A number of years after I sold it, a new owner engaged in a gut renovation that probably cost between $1.5-2.0MM. Nothing was left of the original construction except the exterior walls. However, there was no expansion of the building envelope. Why should such an extensive and costly renovation not be required to contribute towards inclusionary housing, simply because the house was not expanded? 5) In calculating the cost of a renovation, I suggest that we exclude the cost of certain renovations that promote other goals of the city, including the following: i) The cost of converting a home from a wood exterior to stucco or another fire resistant material; ii) The cost of providing a more fire resistant roof; iii) Landscaping costs that promote fire resilience, such as removal of junipers, installation of hardscape in place of turf, and the cost of creating a defensible fire barrier around the house; iv) The cost of converting from oil to electric; v) The cost of installation of electric charging stations. There are more, but these are a few examples. 6) With respect to ADUs, I suggest that all affordable ADUs be excluded from the imposition of any tax, as this is consistent with a number of City goals. 7) One last point. The Nexus study indicates that the average sales price of a small home on a small lot is $1.08MM. Assume a demolition and reconstruction as two 1,250 sf duplexes (2,500 sf total) at $500 per square foot (almost certainly a low number) or $1.25MM. This results in a total cost of $2.33MM, BEFORE architectural fees, City fees, construction interest, brokerage and profit. Assuming a total of those items is $300k (also low), the total cost of this project is $2.66M or $1.33MM for each unit, more than the average cost of a small home on a small lot. In fact, $250,000 more. Can we please stop referring to duplexes as a source of attainable housing, when newly constructed units will cost more than small single -family homes? When I see newly constructed duplexes at $800,000 I will have a different view.

As I will not be present on Thursday, I thought I would offer a few brief comments on the subjects we will be discussing at the Study Session. In that regard, please note the following: Forgive me for being a little bit acerbic (both the Nuggets and the Knicks lost, and I am out of sorts), but I do not regard the Wildfire Protection document as an actionable resource. The executive summary is too short, the bulk of the memo is too long. It is not ??? and should not be - our job to become subject matter experts in this field, certainly not at the level of detail contained in this ???throw in the kitchen sink??? document, and absolutely not within one week. A more focused set of recommendations with specific timelines would have been more useful. 370 pages is an absurd length for a memo; as an action plan in the private sector it would not be considered acceptable. But having stated that, I do have a couple of points to make: As I noted at one of our recent meetings, there are a number of steps that could easily be taken much more quickly than we were led to believe. We were told to expect ordinance changes by, if my memory is correct, 4th quarter of 2025. In my view there is absolutely no reason why we could not much sooner institute an ordinance prohibiting the use of certain building materials in the WUI for new construction or substantial modifications. Similarly, a proscriptive ordinance with respect to future planting of certain types of vegetation in the WUI, such as junipers, should be possible to do now on an expedited basis. It is sometimes possible to overthink simple actions. There are more than a hundred possible actions to be taken (at least), and no guidance as to how they should be prioritized. It would seem to me that creating fire and fuel breaks and removing fuel from around power lines should be a high priority and commence now, but we have been given no analytical framework from which we are able to weight this policy against a multitude of others. Too many of the possible actions come with a ???0-5+??? year timeline. That is not useful. Asking Council to prioritize this multitude of actions is well outside the scope of our competence (with the possible exception, based on her previous experience, of my colleague Taishya Adams) and is properly the responsibility of professionals in the field to provide their suggestions for a specific 5-year action plan. That is a document I would like to see, and to discuss. With respect to the public safety topic, apparently there has been a rise in crime in North Boulder. I believe it would be useful to ask what the plan is for combatting this situation. If one has already been implemented, how is it working? I am confident that you will be well-guided by Councilmember Schuchard on Thursday for a robust discussion of these 2 topics. See everyone at the first meeting in June.

As it was the clear will of Council (not mine, but we act by vote of the majority) to move forward with a Service Area Expansion Plan (the ???????Plan????????) for the Area III Planning Reserve, we were invited to suggest via Hotline some guardrails and considerations for that Plan. Yet another invitation to draft a Hotline? Does it get any better? I am delighted to comply, and I have a few thoughts for that document which I will present here: 1) First and foremost, the Plan must be entirely focused on providing affordable, middle-income and what I will call attainable housing (perhaps a level of $800,000 and under, although the limits are certainly subject to discussion). Not 25% of the housing in these categories, not 40% and not 50%. We need to build the maximum amount of this type of housing possible. Boulder does not need ONE additional unit of market rate housing. We currently have more than enough middle-income rental housing. If you make 80-120% of AMI there are a multitude of rental options available to you. Of course, if you want to purchase a home, good luck. 2)The additional housing units contemplated by the East Boulder rezoning, and the additional density permitted near transit corridors, (virtually all of which are likely to be market rate rentals), can provide more than enough housing to fulfill the requirements of the DRCOG study suggesting that we need an additional 10,000 units of housing. The only point of developing the Planning Reserve is to provide the affordable and missing middle housing, especially units for sale, that we do not produce now. Each market rate unit contemplated by the Plan represents a lost opportunity for this property. 3) I commend to the drafters of the Plan the letter we recently received from Macon Cowles, suggesting a test case development of a small portion of the Planning Reserve dedicated entirely to workforce housing. If the owner of that parcel is prepared to move forward in that manner we should pursue this immediately; it does not require a lengthy study to determine its desirability. If the owner is willing, we should act promptly. 4) I believe we need to rethink using 200 acres for a regional park. We do not count our 47,000 acres of Open Space in addressing the sufficiency of our parkland, but perhaps we should give some credit to our Open Space in making that determination. In addition, Parks and Recreation currently lacks funds to construct and maintain existing parks properties (see the difficulties in financing a satisfactory replacement for the South Boulder Rec Center). The Plan must address the source of funding for developing such a large regional park, as well as an estimate of the cost of its annual maintenance and the source of funding for that maintenance. 5) If we were to be able to utilize some portion of the 200 acres allocated for a regional park for housing (perhaps 100 acres?) we could repay to Parks the amount they have paid for it, and that land could be suitable for affordable and middle-income housing. The Plan should examine that possibility. 6) Water. We are contemplating adding several thousand units of housing in an environment in which this community will have less water in the future, due to two factors. The first is climate change: this winter is a harbinger of what is to come, and we need to account for this. The second is the 7-state compact with respect to the Colorado River. This agreement will be revised either in cooperation with the other 6 states, or by fiat from the federal government. In either case we will have a lower allocation of water from the Colorado. In the second case, given the nature of this administration and its dim view of the State of Colorado, we may end up with substantially less water. The Plan must analyze our prospective water supplies and its impact on this project. 7) Design over quantity. Many people have spoken about the possibilities of a new Holiday neighborhood, or something similar. We should definitely move in this direction. The point is not to cram the maximum number of units of housing into the Reserve, which will require extensive use of stacked flats, but to design walkable neighborhoods that people actually want to live in. Holiday 2 should be the mantra of this development and the theme of the Plan. 8) And now we come to the most important issue: staff has previously estimated that the required infrastructure for the buildout of the Planning Reserve will be somewhere in the range of $600MM-$1BN. That is not a number remotely within our capacity to pay; it is more than double the entire amount that can be raised from our infrastructure tax, or CCRS. The Plan must address the following issues: i) How is it contemplated that this infrastructure bill will be paid? ii) If those costs are to be imposed upon the property owners/developers of Area III properties, how can we possibly achieve any type of affordability, as those units will be burdened with their share of the cost of the contemplated infrastructure? If the infrastructure costs $600MM and we build 6,000 units, the per unit cost would be $100,000. At an infrastructure cost of $1BN, the per unit cost is $166,000. There is an inherent tension between our desire for affordability and our need to have Area III property owners shoulder the burden of paying for new infrastructure. How to resolve? iii) What will be the disruption to the rest of the community from installing the massive new infrastructure necessary to serve this new community? The Plan is the key document in the future development of Area III; we need to get it right. Should we decide to move for\ward after the preparation of the Plan, this will constitute the most important development project of our lifetimes and we must be thoughtful and measured in our approach. And I look forward to our next invitation to communicate via Hotline.

As more and more complaints and anecdotes come in, it is entirely clear that the Xcel response to last weekend???s weather conditions was, to put it kindly, entirely bollixed. I am grateful that CAC has chosen to add a staff briefing on what happened to this week???s Council meeting, and invited Xcel to appear before Council on April 17. As I will definitely miss the meeting this week, and will probably be unavailable next week as well, I want to offer a few suggestions as to some of the questions we might pose to Xcel, and the issues we should raise with them. This was a draconian response to extremely dangerous weather conditions, but I cannot fault Xcel for taking a proactive stance. The memory of the Marshall Fire is all too clear. But this particular response was lacking in execution in so many ways. Only a partial list would include the following: 1) Was this part of a plan or simply an ad hoc act of desperation? If the former, how is it possible that a plan could be rolled out in a climate of total confusion? How could there be so little advance notice of this possibility to Xcel???s client cities and customers, and so little notice to residents and businesses? 2) Further to the prior point, if this was indeed an ad hoc response to weather conditions, and paraphrasing a question that was first asked by my colleague Ryan Schuchard, how is it possible that we do not have in place a fully integrated plan to deal with a situation like we experienced last weekend, a plan that has been formulated with input from all relevant stakeholders? That is not only a good question, but it might well be the critical question. Spoiler alert: this is Colorado, and we occasionally experience gale force winds, among other natural calamities. We expect our public, monopoly provider of electricity to anticipate events such as this and to have a plan in place to address it, one that has been formulated in coordination with local governments and key institutions. 3) How were areas selected to be powered down? Was there any rhyme or reason to those determinations? Were equity considerations even applied to those determinations? I have been told that even one or our hospitals was without power for a while. If this is true, I have to ask: what was Xcel thinking? In my neighborhood of Lower Chautauqua, we lose limbs from old, mature trees in every major snowstorm and windstorm, impacting our elevated power lines and shutting down our electricity. Our power lines are always at risk and our electricity goes out at the drop of a hat (undergrounding, anyone?). Yet we had electricity throughout the weekend (and yes, I am happy about that), while the entire downtown area went dark. But which area would appear to be more resilient to fire: neighborhoods such as mine in the Wildland Urban Interface, or businesses in our downtown area? So what was the theory behind the decisions? 4) Xcel???s strategies have resulted in untold losses to our restaurant industry and supermarkets (among many other businesses). My question to staff is: do we have any way of calculating the magnitude of those losses? That is a figure I would like to know. I question whether Xcel has any idea what it costs in ruined food and lost clientele to shut down a Safeway or a restaurant such as the Cork for a weekend. My question to Xcel is: do you contemplate any restitution to those businesses and to your residential customers who lived in the cold and dark for days? If not, why not? 5) And how is it possible that the electricity for a substantial part of our community can be turned off with the flick of a switch, but turning it back on is like one of the labors of Hercules? There was very little wind on Sunday, none today, but there remain people without power, or have only had their power restored within the last few hours. I suspect that very few people outside of Xcel were initially aware of the disparity between the time it takes to shut the system down and the time it takes to restart it. They do now, though. 6) I would characterize Xcel???s communications with the community as dismal, but that is only because, when posting to Hotline, I try to refrain from using stronger language not fit for a family audience. I believe that people can deal with almost any condition if they are given accurate information as to how long they will have to endure discomfort, and if those deadlines are kept. Deadlines for restoration of power that get extended every time they approach the time for restoration, is not what I consider communication. But even in that event, communicate why the deadline cannot be met, what the problem is, and what the expectations are for moving forward towards restoration. This is just not that hard; at least it should not be. I am sure that my colleagues will have many, many other questions for Xcel when they appear before the Council. Whether Xcel has adequate answers to these questions remains to be seen.

As there is no staff memo in connection with Thursday???s Study Session, there are a few areas that it might be useful to cover with respect to the discussion surrounding methamphetamine and its impact on the community. I am sure that staff is prepared to cover many, most or all of the following, but I wanted to articulate the issues that are of interest to me, and perhaps to a few of my colleagues. Those issues are as follows: 1) What are the current statistics regarding the scope of the meth problem nationally? How does Boulder compare to those national trends? What are the metrics for success/failure? 2) Can we discuss the meth problem demographically? How do rates of addiction compare by age, gender, economic status and ethnicity? How are those figures altered by whether one is housed or not? 3) There is a general impression (by which I really mean, my impression), that there are no effective protocols for the treatment of meth addiction. Is this the case, or are there promising methodologies that we should be pursuing? 4) For those of us (again, me) who are not sufficiently knowledgeable about meth addiction, what are its long-term impacts on addicts in terms of health and behavior? Is there recovery from long-term use, and how much is the prospect of recovery diminished by the length of use? 5) We have experienced the heavy cost of remediation of meth contamination of our public buildings, such as the library. Boulder Housing Partners has experienced the same expense in its affordable home communities. Is there any non-invasive way to test for the presence of meth on an individual consistent with privacy rights? If not, how are businesses supposed to operate in a safe manner for the public and their staff? What protocols should they be establishing for their customers, restrooms or other public spaces? 6) Some of us have longed for the establishment of a treatment center to deal with meth addiction, so as not to simply cycle the addicted through the prison system. What is the track record elsewhere with respect to such facilities (this ties back to my question 2). What is the expense to establish such a facility? At the end of the day, is this a strategy that can effectively be pursued? If so, at what cost and what resources might be available to ameliorate the cost? 7) What percentage of our police resources are dedicated to dealing with the meth problem? Do we have sufficient resources for the task? Public safety has become an overwhelming issue in Boulder. How do we achieve it? This list is not intended to be exhaustive, and I am sure that there are many areas that I have not covered that will be discussed on Thursday. I look forward to that conversation. .

As this is being written in the aftermath of Super Bowl Sunday, it will be mercifully brief. Having read the staff memo in connection with our various programs addressing the problem of homelessness in Boulder, I want to raise the following questions before Thursday (and written responses not necessary before the meeting): 1) To what is the decrease in homelessness (page 3 of the staff memo) attributed? Are there any special factors? 2) Of the many programs being operated within the $9.8MM budget in 2024, which are working best, and would merit additional funds? Which are working least well? What portion of our budget is at risk of being reduced by the federal government? 3) The high utilizer effort has housed approximately 13 of 51 identified high utilizers. What is the total cost of the program as scaled down in 2024 from its original 3-year cost of $8,926,000? What has been the cost of housing and treating those 13 high utilizers, both in total and per capita? 4) I do not see the cost of the voucher program with BHP included in the budget. Is this the line item of $1,021,875 and listed only as ???????local vouchers????????? 5) When do we expect to receive an analysis of the success of Project Recovery from the Omni Research Firm? Do we have any early indications of the results? 6) As I understand it, with individual payments of $6,000/year and a total capacity to fund up to $3MM, Elevate Boulder can serve up to 500 people/year. Just as a matter of leverage, how many individuals could be served if that expenditure were to be allocated among EFFA, EPRAS, All Roads and an expansion of the HOT team? While there is no doubt that the Elevate Boulder payments have the most profound effect for its recipients, would helping the largest number of individuals not be a better alternative? How are we analyzing this? My recollection is that this program was funded through ARPA funds. If it is intended to continue this program going forward, what will be the source of its funding? 7) Attached to the staff memo is the 2024 Public Policy Associates evaluation of the Homeless Solutions for Boulder County (HSBC) system. The staff memo notes that ???????The consultant explores the possibility of alternate shelter models, such as sanctioned encampments and safe parking programs??????????????? That analysis is directed towards the County and its land assets, but does staff intend it to be equally directed towards the City of Boulder? If so, will there be consideration and analysis of Boulder????????s lack of available land, the cost thereof, and the particular expenses of operating in this jurisdiction? As I recall, we did this analysis with respect to high utilizers, and the per capita expense was shocking in its anticipated cost. As we consider whether to move forward with any community needs study related to Area 3 annexation, I want to offer a recommendation on how we scope that work from the outset. My strong preference is that staff narrow the focus of any study to middle-income, medium-density ownership housing, specifically, homes in the 1,200 to 1,500 square foot range, priced to be attainable for working households. The model I have in mind is well-established right here in our region: Boulder????????s own Holiday neighborhood and Prospect in Longmont are examples of what thoughtfully designed, moderately-scaled for-sale housing can look like when it????????s done well. What I am not interested in studying is additional apartment rental inventory or high-end luxury product. Boulder has seen plenty of both, and neither addresses the housing gap that is at the heart of this conversation. To test whether real demand exists before committing significant staff time and resources to a full study, I????????d propose starting with a targeted survey targeting 2 groups. First, survey city employees across all departments including city staff, police, fire, and teachers who currently live outside Boulder city limits, and ask a simple, direct question: if you could purchase a roughly 1,500 square foot home in Area 3 for approximately $750,000, deed restricted to limit resale appreciation to 3% per year plus a COLA adjustment, would you choose to live in Boulder? Second, extend that same question to the rest of the estimated 60,000 people who commute into the city for work each day. I recognize that Boulder has surveyed in-commuters before, but regional housing stock and sentiment has shifted considerably in recent years and current data is essential before making assumptions about demand that could drive a major land use decision. At its core, this effort is about two interconnected goals: reducing the burden of in-commuting on our transportation network and environment, and building a stronger, more complete community where the people who serve and support Boulder can also afford to live here. If the demonstrated demand falls short of the housing capacity being contemplated, we should pause the idea until demand is clearly demonstrated rather than proceed on assumptions alone. I????????d welcome a conversation with staff about how to structure this efficiently before any broader study is launched. Get Outlook for iOS

At last Thursday????????s meeting I put aside a request for a nod of five to exempt affordable housing from the new Transportation Maintenance Fee until staff could analyze its impact on the revenues to be generated and the problems of establishing this exemption. Boulder Housing Partners, our largest provider of affordable housing, has approximately 2,000 units that it is operating. As almost all of them are in multi-family structures, at $42/unit, it would seem to me that the lost revenue from this exemption, if enacted, would be approximately $84,000 out of the anticipated revenue of $6.423MM, when the program is fully up and running, or 1.3% of the anticipated revenue. This leads me to ask the following: Is my calculation correct with respect to the BHP units? How many additional units of affordable housing do we have in Boulder, and what would the deduction look like for them? If the total deduction is more than we would care to bear, perhaps we can consider a reduced payment/unit, rather than a full deduction, as we do for several other categories against which we assess the TMF. I await staff????????s analysis.

At long last. Since the morning after the 2021 disturbance on the Hill, when then Councilmember Rachel Friend and I went down to assess the damage, we became advocates for some form of chronic nuisance ordinance to address the most problematic properties and egregious behaviors. Although in a perfect world we would have done this in under 3 years, the fact that it is getting done at all is a small miracle. And I am pleased that staff ignored my impatience and pleas for greater speed and reached out to so many stakeholders and received such serious input from each of them. This is as well-vetted a piece of legislation as I can remember. This strikes me as an extremely well-drafted Ordinance (more on that shortly), and I have only a few comments or proposed revisions. These are set forth below, but first I want to again thank everyone involved in tackling this very difficult problem so well. My few comments are as follows: 1) The near-term check-in is very important, but given the time necessary for setting up systems, public education, and the like, will 18 months provide enough time to usefully collect data? Would 2 years serve the purpose better? 2) You have previously received correspondence from a coalition of community groups, led by the Chamber and Boulder Housing Partners, who are concerned that without an exemption or special categorization for Permanently Supportive Housing or Transitional Housing, this statute could have a chilling effect on the production of such housing. Your unwillingness to accommodate these concerns is perplexing to me, and when I see the Chamber aligning with BHP, EFAA and All Roads (the Shelter), I tend to sit up and take notice. The only rationale in the memo for this reluctance is that ???Staff does not support exempting any properties from this ordinance.??? This is a statement of preference, not a reason, and none are offered. Why not? And it is promised that you will work with housing providers to avoid an adverse outcome, which is essentially saying ???Don???t worry about your concerns, we will take care of it.??? For an operator of this type of badly needed housing this is thin gruel, indeed. I would request that staff reconsider the exemption, or be more specific as to how the particular needs of these housing providers will be accommodated. I urge you not to let the desire for consistency in treatment of all properties create an adverse climate for the production of this type of housing. 3) I am also aware of BHP???s concern that many of its larger, dense housing developments could too easily fall into the chronic nuisance category, often due to efforts to house those who were previously homeless, and may have more difficulty acclimatizing to the new environment. I know that staff has received extensive correspondence on this issue. Have recent conversations resolved those concerns or does this remain an open issue? If the latter, I hope that this issue can be addressed as well. 4) P. 7, refers to the change in terms from ???violations??? to ???outstanding violations???. Does this imply that the slate is wiped clean when violations are cured? Is there no impact to a history of poor behavior, at least within the last few years? 5) Given the potential drain on resources, particularly the police department, why were calls for service excluded from the calculation of public nuisance? 6) Section 10-2.5-1, Legislative Findings, is very clearly drafted and the drafters should be commended. 7) The statutory language excusing violations reported to a police authority by a property manager is confusing to me. This occurs on page 16 of the staff memo and in the Definitions section of the Ordinance. That language reads as follows: ???Violations that are first reported to a peace officer by a person having an ownership or leasehold interest in the parcel where a violation or violations have occurred, or having a contractual obligation to manage such parcel, or occupying such parcel may not be deemed public nuisances under this chapter.??? Does this imply that a property owner or agent can simply inform on themselves to the police, and the underlying conduct is excused from the calculation of whether that property is a chronic nuisance offender? Please explain. 8) I am unclear as to the impact of a property conveyance (Page 30 of the Memo, Section 10-2.5-25 of the Ordinance.) Does this wipe the slate clean even if the conditions to be corrected are still in place? Why is the new owner not taking subject to existing, uncorrected nuisances? And would it not make sense to exempt any such property purchased by a public housing authority, as they will surely be attempting to bring the property up to code? 9) I know that BARHA is requesting that when a notice goes out to the property owner, the holder of the rental license should also be noticed. This strikes me as a reasonable request. If, as anticipated, only a few of the most difficult properties will be noticed of their violation of this ordinance, it does not seem to me to be unduly burdensome to copy the notice and send it to the holder of the license. Please consider addressing some of the issues I have raised in this Hotline; with these few reservations, I am delighted to get so close to the end of a very long journey to improve life in Boulder.

At our next Council meeting we will be addressing the issue of a sanctioned campground in Boulder. Having read the staff memo on this subject, I must say that there is a great deal of additional information I believe we require in order to make a reasoned decision on this subject. At the moment, we appear to be pursuing a solution based on an instinctive belief that it is the proper course of action, without much data in support of that decision, or analysis as to why it is better than other alternatives. Among the many questions I have (along with some comments) are the following: 1) On pages 3-4 of the staff memo are listed 11 separate programs currently addressing homelessness. What is the cumulative expense of these programs over the past 2- 3 years? What has been their cumulative impact in reducing homelessness? How many individuals have they served? If they have a track record of effectiveness, it would certainly be imprudent to cannibalize their funding for a program addressing the needs of 30 individuals. What is the reality? 2) One of our Homelessness Strategic Goals (p. 3 of the memo) is to ???Support an efficient and effective services system based on best practices and data.??? Accordingly, what constitutes best practices and what is the data upon which we are proceeding? How can we make an informed determination in the absence of this information? 3) When we first began to address this subject a couple of years ago, staff was adamant that sanctioned campgrounds were not an effective strategy for combatting homelessness. What has changed since then? Has this now become the accepted best practice for addressing homelessness, and, if so, why? Has this Council become so sure of its judgment that it not only overrides that of staff, but requires no data or support for doing so? 4) The memo mentions four municipalities that appear to have had some success with this strategy. What is the data on which this definition of success is based? How many of those who have utilized those facilities have exited homelessness? Is the number of exits larger than what would have been expected from other programs? What has been the average length of stay in those facilities? How do they define a successful outcome? Should those be our standards? 5) What of the other municipalities? How many cities who have established sanctioned campgrounds have abandoned the effort? Have we been cherry-picking the cities to support a desired result? When the memo states that ???Alternate shelter programs have been growing as a method to increase sheltering capacity?????? what exactly does that mean? How many cities? How many individuals served? What has changed over the past couple of years to make this a successful solution in contrast to those cities in which this course of action has been unsuccessful? 6) Check my math: If we elect to develop the palette program with full services, the cost of erecting the structures (based on a program serving 30 individuals; is this correct?) comes out to $30,000 per individual for set-up and $7,000 per individual for maintenance in future years. Assuming the costs for providing full services is also based on a program for 30 individuals (is it?) the cost for those services in year 1 would be an additional $36,766 per person and $37,557 thereafter. If these assumptions are correct, the total expenditure appears to be about $66,700 per individual for set-up and an ongoing expenditure of more than $44,500 per individual in subsequent years. And this cost is WITHOUT factoring in the cost of land (a permanent parcel will ultimately have to be acquired). As private parcels of land often sell for $2-3MM/acre, we are now looking at a program with services that could ultimately cost well over $100,000 for each individual served. Is this a correct estimate? Even if we opted for ice fishing tents and more limited services, the cost would be $38,200 per individual for year 1 and an ongoing expense of $37,800 in subsequent years (again, without factoring in land cost). And we know that far more than 30 individuals would ultimately require shelter and services. If so, that leads me to ask: What is the real cost of this program based on the real need, or are we to assume that 30 spaces are all we will require and 30 individuals are all we will serve? And this is the core issue with respect to this project: are we properly leveraging our scarce dollars on this effort? What, for instance, could EFAA and Bridge House do with an extra $1-$1.5MM each? How many more could they serve, or prevent from entering homelessness? Is $3MM-$4MM (including the cost of land) to serve 30 individuals the appropriate use of our resources, when there are so many programs who serve vast multiples of 30 individuals? 7) The analysis of potential sites for this facility is useful, but where is the staff recommendation as to which site makes the most sense? No insult to us, but asking the Council to serve as the real estate selection committee, with our limited subject matter experience in this field, makes about as much sense as asking your plumber to perform your open heart surgery. The result might be excellent, but you really would not want to count on it. What is staff???s view of the matter? 8) And, if we do go down this path, do we even have a metric by which to determine that the project is a success? A failure? If this project will be judged by exits from homelessness, how many will be required to justify the commitment? Do we even know? 9) Finally, I have to note that the manner in which we are approaching this is a continuation of our repeated failure to approach budgetary issues holistically. We look at each issue in isolation, determine that the cause or purpose of spending is just and approve it without reference to any other spending initiatives we have chosen to support. Recently, we have approved a program to Reimagine Policing, that will ultimately require additional funds for additional staffing for that department. As a result of the passage of the 2023 ballot initiative approximately $1.8MM/year (or more) will no longer be available to the General Fund. Under the Facilities Master Plan there is an expectation of additional funding of $6.2MM per year to better maintain our infrastructure, as well as dedicating (???ring fencing???) operational savings from improved structures (not yet quantified) towards future capital asset maintenance. We are moving forward with a $3MM Guaranteed Income Project with ARPA funding. Could this program jeopardize expenditures for that one, after the ARPA money has been spent? Or, in the ultimate irony, could the financial requirements for this program endanger funding for the day shelter? In sum, I am very concerned that the request to spend over $3MM-$4MM (including land cost) for a program for 30 members of the unhoused community (a program that many of its members most in need of services will not utilize) is not consistent with an integrated funding strategy, lacks the data to support its initiation and will require HHS to make it a reality at the expense of existing and proven programs. I would be entirely supportive of a program that is supported by data to demonstrate its potential for success, and one that we can actually implement at a price that does not require us to cannibalize other programs. At the moment we lack the data to support a positive a response to the first concern, and have more than enough data to create concern about the second. We may approve moving forward because we believe this project is humane (it certainly is), but acting almost entirely on our emotional values is governance by impulse, not reason.

City Council Members, As you are aware, Xcel Energy filed a Phase 1 electric rate case in December 2022, proposing to increase the base rate revenue requirement by $312.2 million, which, if approved, would have resulted in an 8.2% bill increase for residents, a 7.77% increase for small commercial customers and a 5-7% increase for large commercial and industrial customers. Xcel Energy also proposed to increase its authorized return on equity from 9.3 percent to 10.25 percent. The City of Boulder intervened in this proceeding and is represented by staff from the City Attorney???s Office and the Department of Climate Initiatives. The city filed testimony advocating for a reduced return on equity and for development of a roadmap to reduce energy insecurity for all residential customers, such that utility bills represented no more than four percent of total annual household income. The city also supported exploring performance-based ratemaking as a strategy to help shift Xcel Energy???s financial incentives away from more capital investment and toward improved customer service and resilience of the current system. Late yesterday afternoon, Xcel Energy, Trial Staff of the Public Utilities Commission, the Office of Utility Consumer Advocates, Colorado Energy Consumers, the Colorado Energy Office, Molson Coors Beverage Company, Walmart and the Federal Executive Agencies reached a near-comprehensive settlement. While the remaining parties (the City and County of Denver, Climax Molybdenum Company, the Coalition for Community Solar Access, the Board of Water Works for Pueblo, and Kroger Company) are taking no position on this settlement, the City Attorney???s Office and city staff have decided to oppose the settlement. The parties did make substantial progress in negotiating a lower revenue requirement and return on equity; however, the net result of the settlement would still be a rate increase for all customers while preserving or even increasing profits for Xcel Energy. There is also uncertainty around two issues ??? depreciation costs associated with coal plan retirements (Comanche 3, Craig 2, Hayden 1, Hayden 2 and Pawnee) and aspects of the Transmission Cost Adjustment (the projects that can be included and whether to shift the methodology to cost recovery of actuals from the current forward estimation used currently) - that were not resolved as part of the settlement that would further impact rates. Given the extensive concerns raised by our community in written public comment to the Commission as well as feedback staff have gathered through community engagement, the decision was made that the city would oppose the settlement. Staff do truly appreciate the efforts of the parties in this case and very much support the settlement process as a general strategy. As staff reflected on this over the last several days, however, we realized that in these unprecedented times, it???s important for the Commission to take our community???s concerns into account as they consider whether to accept the settlement. Some of the key issues informing staff???s position: The settlement supports increasing the weighted average cost of capital (WACC), which is the cost to finance infrastructure investments. The WACC is comprised of the cost of short-term and long-term debt as well as the cost of shareholder equity. While staff agree that current economic conditions are contributing to a higher cost of debt, the proposed WACC would result in a higher equity return than that set by recent precedent in two other states that Xcel serves. Additionally, setting the WACC serves as precedent that may carry forward irrespective of the future cost of debt. The settlement would carry forward Xcel???s current allowable return on equity. The community has expressed strong concern over Xcel???s profits in Colorado. Staff also do not believe that this level of return is necessary for Xcel as evidenced by their financial condition and history over the last five years, which was reflected in the city???s testimony. In presenting rate case impacts, Xcel utilizes an average customer bill impact methodology. This methodology masks the impact of rate increases on customers whose bills already represent a substantial portion of their income. This past year has seen a dramatic increase in customers seeking energy assistance funding, an issue that has been raised in several proceedings at both the State General Assembly and the Public Utilities Commission. There is a need for better analysis and transparency on bill impacts within this and future rate cases, as well as a firm commitment for establishing a roadmap for reducing customer energy insecurity. Xcel spent $2.2 million in preparing and litigating this rate case and seeks to recover these costs from customers. In settling items and deferring other items to future rate cases, it can be argued that the need for this rate case and, subsequently the need to incur those expenses, is unjustified. The city filed both answer testimony and cross answer testimony in this proceeding, making recommendations on the return on equity, energy insecurity, performance-based ratemaking and other topics. Attached, please find a copy of the settlement, as filed with the Commission. Please do not hesitate to contact me should you have any questions or concerns. Sincerely, Jonathan Jonathan Koehn Director (pronouns: He/Him/His) What's This?
