City Council Members, At this week???s council agenda meeting, committee members asked that staff outline the process sequence for the proposed annexation and site review at 5961 S. Boulder Rd. First reading of the annexation resolution and ordinance appear on the Dec. 21, 2023 consent agenda (item 3H), while the companion site review application appears on the call up agenda (item 4B). Adoption of an annexation resolution is simply a procedural step required under state law to determine that the petition to annex the property complies with section 30(1)(c) of article II of the state constitution and section 31-12-107(1), C.R.S., and to set a public hearing date (second reading of the ordinance) to determine if the proposed annexation complies with state annexation laws. A public hearing for the annexation is scheduled for Feb. 1, 2024, and the second reading of the annexation ordinance will be scheduled at the same time. If council finds after the public hearing that the proposed annexation complies with state annexation laws, council could adopt the annexation ordinance to annex the property. If the site review, which is altogether a separate application, is called-up by City Council, the public hearing for that application would be scheduled concurrently with the public hearing and second reading of the proposed annexation ordinance on Feb. 1, 2024. If the item is not called up, City Council cannot consider or render a decision on the Site Review application, since the site review approval would then become final following expiration of the call-up period. The site review approval is conditioned upon adoption of the proposed annexation ordinance and would expire if the proposed annexation ordinance were not adopted. If council would like to consider the site review along with the annexation, staff recommends that council call up the Site Review application. Please note that a majority vote of council is required to call-up the site review for a public hearing. As mentioned above, if the site review is not called-up, the Planning Board approval will stand, although council approval of the annexation will be required to effectuate the site review approval. Recognizing this is a bit of a unique and somewhat complex process, staff is happy to meet with council members individually if there are procedural questions. City Councilmembers: At your regular meeting on May 1, 2025, members of the community spoke to the current code compliance activity taking place at the Sage School. Per your request, following is a summary of the history of enforcement: The Sage School is located at 1545 Upland in North Boulder. The city responded to two separate complaints in February 2025 from two community members, who expressed concerns in particular regarding the safety and construction of some of the buildings. Upon inspection, building code and zoning violations were discovered. The zoning on the property is Residential Estate (RE). The use on the property is school, which is defined in the Boulder Municipal Code as follows: School, elementary, middle, or high means any public or private school for any grades between first and twelfth which satisfies state compulsory education requirements. The school has full-day classes (regular school year listed, as well as summer programs), multiple teachers, multiple grade levels being taught, and tuition charges. Private schools are an allowed use within the RE Zone District through a Use Review. The process takes about 90 days and is subject to Planning Board call up. Staff has offered to assist the Sage School in submitting an application, which can be processed while they address the building code violations. Staff has also shared the assessment that the criteria for a Use Review can very likely be met (while respecting that it ultimately remains a quasi-judicial decision of Planning Board/Council). The school has not yet submitted an application. The building code violations range in location and scale. Following are some of the issues found during inspection, some of which the property owners are currently working on, with assistance from the city: A number of unpermitted buildings: an Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) without permits in a barn, a partially conditioned shed (interior finish including electric), a deck without permits (needing guardrails and handrails), and an attached greenhouse on the front of the main structure, built without permits. The property also has a large yurt with a support deck/platform constructed without permits. The yurt is being removed and sold off. They may be removing the deck/platform or work to have it permitted. There is a high risk of fire on the property from multiple stacks of improperly stored materials. There are play structures that may not comply with a review by for schools by the State Licensing Agency. (Staff is working with the State to understand any separate actions they may be undertaking.) Staff continue to work with school officials to correct the building violations. We are hopeful that the owners will begin to work with staff to submit a Use Review of approval. Concerning Council????????s resolution on a vision and conditions to continue exploring Area III service area expansion (original draft below), I propose four additions: #1. Use the low cost of the area????????s land value to support significant levels of new permanently affordable, deed-restricted housing for ownership at the middle range of affordability (i.e., ~50-150% AMI). Considerations: One of the clearest ways the planning reserve can potentially contribute to housing goals in a way that is unique is by contributing the value of city-owned land to reduce total housing costs and pass that subsidy on to future residents. The ability to do that would seem to depend on significant value remaining after costs like infrastructure which are expected to be up to ~$1,000,000,000 per the services study are expended. A principle for going forward should be that significant land value, net of infrastructure and other costs, is available to support the creation of permanently affordable, deed-restricted housing for ownership at the middle range of affordability (i.e., around 50-150% of area median income), and used for that purpose. #2. Maximally support car-free living for all inhabitants. Considerations: Some current residents are understandably concerned about the potential for car traffic and surrounding problems to increase with a sharp increase to population in one part of town if a more people-centered outcome is not managed for. On the other hand, the planning profession shows that better infrastructure and services for transit, bikeability, and walkability are key to overcoming traffic woes????????and greater density actually enables that process. However, the best outcomes are not automatic????????we have to plan for them. Developing Area III is an opportunity to design a community that gives people of all ages, abilities, and incomes the ability to thrive without a car, while leveraging new inhabitants to improve the economics of public and active transportation for the whole community. A principle for going forward should be that the subcommunity will be designed to encourage and allow all inhabitants to live without a car, with consideration of the community itself and how it connects to wider Boulder and the region. #3. Forbid new fossil fuel infrastructure, including natural gas. Considerations: Consistent with Boulder????????s climate action plan and 2026 policy statement, both adopted recently by Council, Boulder must ratchet down the use of fossil fuels down and certainly not expand their use. The development of new subcommunities such as with Area III is when we have the greatest opportunity to develop all-electric, clean, world-class designs and infrastructure; conversely, it????????s when we face the greatest threat of locking in fossil systems that are incompatible with our climate, sustainability, and resilience by doing things like we????????ve done before. Future planning for the site must exclude the possibility of building new natural gas infrastructure. #4. As part of validating a potential case to develop the planning reserve, provide an alternative investment scenario to make use of the proposed funding (which includes up to ~$1,000,000,000 per the services study) and other associated costs to develop housing as urban infill instead. Considerations: Council????????s decision about Area III on February 12 was to take the next step in exploration based on need and did not consider a full picture of costs, opportunity costs, or the expectation of benefits net of other considerations. It????????s a reasonable hypothesis that the large amounts of resources involved in potential expansion (including up to ~$1,000,000,000 per the services study) could be put to use for strategies that could secure the same outcomes for less cost through infill within the city????????s current service area, where existing infrastructure, services, and proximities support cost advantages and other synergies. Council Colleagues & City Staff: I appreciate city staff submitting yesterday afternoon a supplemental memo for Thursday night's council meeting, reminding council that we have already discussed the disposition of the city's library buildings. Staff correctly identified that council discussion as occurring on March 15, 2022, a few months before the community voted on whether to form a library district and approve a new library property tax (which the voters did that November). There actually was an earlier council discussion on this question on February 8, 2022, but the focused council discussion on the disposition of the library buildings occurred on March 15. At the March 15 discussion, all eight council members (Junie was absent) agreed that the city should not transfer ownership of the downtown main library building, if a library district was formed. The recording of that March 15 council meeting can be viewed here (relevant discussion beginning at 1:33). On the question of whether the city should transfer vs. lease the three branch library buildings (Carnegie, Reynolds, and North), council was somewhat split. Four council members (Rachel, Mark, Tara and Bob) said that, for the same reason that the city should not transfer the main library building to a new library district, the city should not transfer the branch library buildings either. However, four council members (Nicole, Lauren, Matt, and Aaron) said that night that they would be open to a further discussion about the branch library buildings at the appropriate time. Aaron helpfully summarized the results of that March 15 council discussion, which can be seen on the recording at 2:56, and Library Director David Farnan acknowledged at 2:59 that the transfer of ownership of the main library building was off the table. I realize that council always has the prerogative to change its mind. But, in this case, council made a pretty clear and unanimous statement (at least as to the main library) that we would not transfer the library building in the event that a library district was approved by the voters a few months later. It is probably fair to assume that some of the voters relied on that council declaration when they cast their ballots on the formation of the library district later that year. I would ask city staff to be prepared at Thursday night's discussion to speak to what would happen to the city's library buildings if they are transferred by the city to the library district under the following scenarios: What would happen if the library buildings are transferred by the city to the library district and the district then pledges the buildings as collateral security for debt incurred by the library district? Such a collateral pledge of the library buildings could be accomplished by the library district in any number of legal ways, including through a traditional mortgage, certificates of participation, or a sale-leaseback involving the library district's lender. I ask city staff to be prepared to advise council at Thursday's council meeting what might happen to the library buildings in the event of a default by the library district in the debt for which the library buildings serve as collateral security. Even if the library district does not pledge the library buildings as collateral security for debt, would a creditor of the library district have recourse to the district-owned library buildings to satisfy a judgement against the library district? What would happen to the library buildings owned by the library district if the district files for federal bankruptcy protection? Contrast that disposition of district-owned buildings in bankruptcy vs. if the buildings are leased to the library district and section 365 of the Bankruptcy Code comes into play. Finally, if council decides to re-affirm its earlier direction that the main library building be leased to the library district, I would appreciate city staff advising council on the terms under which such lease of the building could be for 30 years, rather than the typical city maximum lease term of 20 years. I believe that, in 2012, the voters authorized 30-year city leases under Chapter 111 of the City Charter, which terms are codified under Chapter 10 of Article 8 of the Boulder Revised Code. I'm sure that city council and the community would appreciate hearing from city staff on how a 30-lease of the library building could be accomplished. Best, Bob

Council Colleagues and City Staff Members, I????????d like to share a few suggestions to help our meetings run more smoothly and predictably ???????? related to meeting timing and open comment. First, I believe we should consistently address hate speech and dehumanizing remarks immediately after a speaker has finished. While this wouldn't require a rule change, having the presiding officer clearly state when speech violates our rules, and affirm our council's respect for those being disparaged, immediately after the speaker has finished, would send a strong and timely message. I think this is the most effective and efficient way to uphold our standards when a comment crosses the line but doesn????????t disrupt the meeting outright. On the topic of actual disruptions, we????????re currently using notifications and temporary suspensions from the Penfield Tate building to ensure we can conduct city business effectively. This approach????????limiting in-person attendance while preserving remote access????????already appears to be reducing disruptions, even in the short time it????????s been in place. Finally, I????????d like to propose a small but meaningful structural change: adding a scheduled break between open comment and the rest of our agenda. Specifically, we could begin open comment at 5:30 p.m., then recess until 6:30 p.m. for the rest of the meeting. This would make the start time of our scheduled public hearings more predictable????????helping community members participate in discussions on items we????????re voting on and allowing them to avoid open comment if they prefer. Thanks for considering these ideas. I look forward to discussing them further on Thursday, Lauren Folkerts Mayor Pro Tem Boulder City Council

White; Regents Lori Bergen, Andra Mull, and Robyn Fergus; University Secretary Effie Ameen; Executive Director of Alumni Engagement Ryan Chreist; HLC President Barbara Gellman-Danley; Executive Director of the Colorado Department of Higher Education Angie Paccione; Colorado Commissioner of Education Susana C????rdova; and Members of the Colorado State Board of Education: Please be advised that the University of Colorado Boulder's decision to promote and brand a Martin Luther King Jr. Convocation event featuring Ibram X. Kendi raises serious concerns regarding the ideological misuse of Dr. King's legacy, the abandonment of viewpoint neutrality, and the continuation of a broader pattern of politicized programming under the University's official authority [1]. This objection is not to the commemoration of Dr. King. It is to the deliberate conflation of Dr. King's civil-rights philosophy with a contemporary ideological framework that directly contradicts the principles Dr. King articulated and the constitutional foundations his work helped secure [2]. Dr. King argued for equal dignity under the law, individual moral agency, and the rejection of racial classification as a governing principle. He explicitly warned against replacing one form of racial hierarchy with another and grounded his advocacy in universal civil rights, moral persuasion, and equality before the law [3][4]. By contrast, Dr. Kendi has stated, in his own words, that "the only remedy to racist discrimination is antiracist discrimination," that policies must be evaluated solely by racial outcomes rather than intent or neutrality, and that claims of neutrality are themselves racist [5][6]. These positions reject equal-protection principles and eliminate the possibility of legitimate disagreement. They are not an extension of Dr. King's philosophy; they are philosophically and legally incompatible with it [7]. These concerns are compounded by Dr. Kendi's recent record as an academic leader. As founder and former director of the Center for Antiracist Research at Boston University, Dr. Kendi oversaw an initiative that raised tens of millions of dollars while producing limited peer-reviewed scholarship and ultimately became the subject of extensive public scrutiny. Reporting documented widespread staff departures, allegations of mismanagement, governance failures, and the effective collapse of the Center as a functioning research institution. Dr. Kendi subsequently stepped away from leadership amid internal review and public criticism [8][9][10]. These developments raise serious questions about academic rigor, institutional stewardship, and the prudence of presenting Dr. Kendi as a scholarly or moral authority under the banner of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Presenting Dr. Kendi as a featured voice at an MLK-branded university event is therefore not neutral, historical, or educational. It reframes Dr. King's legacy to endorse a modern ideological doctrine that conflicts with the obligations imposed on public universities under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and long-standing equal-protection jurisprudence [11][12]. This concern does not exist in isolation. Rather, it reflects a pattern of ideological programming at CU Boulder in which contested political frameworks are advanced through official university channels as moral imperatives rather than subjects of academic inquiry, including but not limited to: ??????? University-sponsored DEI programming that frames neutrality and color-blind equal treatment as inherently suspect or harmful [13] ??????? Speaker series and institutional messaging that present outcome-based racial frameworks as settled truth rather than contested theory [14] ??????? Official communications and trainings that encourage "alignment" and "commitment" to specific ideological positions, while marginalizing dissent as moral failure rather than protected academic disagreement [15] In this context, the selection of Dr. Kendi as an MLK Convocation speaker is not incidental. It is consistent with a broader institutional approach that deploys civil-rights language to legitimize a single political worldview while disfavoring alternative interpretations of civil-rights history, constitutional equality, and liberal democratic norms. Search and Rescue Satellite Aided Tracking (SARSAT)

A Beacon of Hope to Those in Distress

NOAA??satellites do more than just monitor the weather. They also detect and relay distress signals from emergency beacons??to the appropriate search and rescue authorities. This tells them who is in trouble and, more importantly, where they are located.

The??NOAA???SARSAT program??is part of COSPAS???SARSAT, an international satellite-based monitoring initiative to which 45 nations and independent search and rescue organizations belong. Using this system, authorities can locate beacons almost anywhere in the world at any time, and in almost any condition.??

COSPAS stands for??"COsmicheskaya??Sisteyama??Poiska??Avariynich??Sudov," Russian for?????Space System for the Search of Vessels in Distress.?????

A sailor being rescued at sea.

SARSAT Tracking Application

Each icon on this map represents one rescue event within the U.S. Area of Responsibility (AOR) in the last 14 months, though multiple saves may be involved with each event.??

The Search and Rescue Satellite Aided Tracking (SARSAT) system is able to detect three types of beacons: an individual???s Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs), maritime Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacons (EPIRBs), and aircraft Emergency Locator Transmitters (ELTs).??

Who responds to the search and rescue are dictated by the location of the distress. For any beacon activation that occurs in the U.S. AOR, the U.S. is responsible for responding. If it is inland, U.S. Air Force responds*, if it is at sea, the U.S. Coast Guard.??

If a device registered to another country is activated within the U.S. AOR, the U.S. is still responsible for the rescue but their homeport country will be notified of the event. All areas of the world are covered by COSPAS-SARSAT.


The COSPAS???SARSAT Program

This program consists of:??

  • Emergency beacons that transmit distress signals
  • Satellites that detect the distress signals
  • Ground receiving stations that receive and process the satellite signals to generate distress alerts
  • Mission control centers that receive the alerts and forward them to rescue coordination centers, operated by the U.S. Coast Guard and the U.S. Air Force.

The U.S. SARSAT system uses NOAA satellites in low-earth and geostationary orbits as well as GPS satellites in medium earth orbit to detect and locate aviators, mariners, and land-based users in distress. The satellites relay distress signals from emergency beacons to a network of ground stations and ultimately to the U.S. Mission Control Center (USMCC) in Suitland, Maryland.

Types of search and rescue beacons.

??

The Four Agencies Involved in the U.S. SARSAT Program

  • NOAA:??System Operation and representative to COSPAS-SARSAT
  • NASA:??Research and Development??
  • U.S. Coast Guard:??Maritime Search and Rescue??
  • U.S. Air Force:??Inland Search and Rescue

??

History

Credit: Arizona Daily Star

The first beacons used the existing 121.5/243 MHz emergency locator transmitters (ELTs) designed for military aircraft in the 1950s. After a small plane carrying Rep. Hale Boggs (D-La.) along with Rep. Nick Begich (D-Alaska) and others disappeared in Alaska in 1972, Congress mandated ELTs on all U.S. aircraft. Canada soon did the same.??

However, early models were not as easy to detect, and there was no way to identify a specific beacon or find its exact location. Thus, engineers began developing new, more robust digital beacons that operated at 406 MHz. Signals from these new beacons could be received from anywhere on the planet, located accurately and almost instantly, and rescue forces would know who and what to look for.

The United States and Canada began looking for other international partners with the ability to launch satellites to achieve a truly global distress alerting satellite system. Russia and France soon signed on to help develop the system for humanitarian purposes.??

On June 30, 1982, Russia launched the first experimental COSPAS???SARSAT satellite. Before it was even officially declared operational, the first distress signal was detected???a downed Canadian aircraft. Within the first hundred days of the satellite???s operation, seven people were rescued using the system. Soon after, NASA launched their own SARSAT payload on NOAA-8. The program has continued to grow ever since.??

Today, with newer, more advanced beacons and a global network of next generation satellites, COSPAS???SARSAT strives to keep improving its ability to take the ???search??? out of ???search and rescue??? and ultimately save lives.??

??

Important Information

All U.S. coded beacons MUST be registered with NOAA.??Read our registration brochure to learn more.??

Safety Notices

  • Airworthiness Directives
  • Ameri-King Corporation ELTs
  • Warning regarding unapproved beacon batteries
  • Kannad SAFELINK EPIRB recall

On 01 February 2025 at 2246 UTC (1746 EST) a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB) was detected at 70 38.5N 157 29.9W, 11 miles north of Atqasuk, AK. It was activated when an individual became lost in the wilderness due to poor visibility. The Alaska Rescue Coordination Center received the alert and contacted North Slope Borough Search and Rescue, which deployed a ground team to the coordinates. The distressed individual was located and transported to his home in Atqasuk, AK.

On 01 February 2026 at 2020 UTC (1520 EDT) an Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) was detected at 29 24N 72 10.8W, 463 NM east of Daytona Beach, FL. It was activated when the sailing vessel MISCHIEF MANAGED, with 3 people on board, began taking on water. USCG Southeast District received the alert, issued an Enhanced Group Call, and launched a rescue plane from Air Station Clearwater to the coordinates. Upon arrival, the aircraft attempted to pass a dewatering pump to the MISCHIEF MANAGED without success and issued a Pan-Pan call requesting assistance from nearby vessels. Motor tanker RADIANT PRIDE responded, arrived on scene, and after several attempts, embarked the uninjured crew members, who will be transported to the vessel's next port of call in Spain.

On 01 June 2025 at 0126 UTC (2126 EDT) a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB) was detected at 36 04.9N 112 08.0W, 2 miles northeast of Grand Canyon Village, AZ. It was activated by a hiker who needed medical assistance. The Air Force Rescue Coordination center received the alert and contacted the Arizona Department of Emergency and Military Affairs, which dispatched the Grand Canyon National Park Service to the coordinates. The hiker was located and transported to a local hospital.

On 01 June 2025 at 1526 UTC (1126 EDT) an Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon (EPIRB) was detected at 28 36.5N 90 16.2W, 29 NM south of Port Fourchon, LA. It was activated after the fishing vessel FILTHY HOOKER, with 3 people on board, began taking on water. Coast Guard District 8 received a call from the captain describing the situation, requested the EPIRB activation, and deployed a helicopter and rescue boat to the coordinates. The assets arrived on scene and the rescue boat escorted FILTHY HOOKER safely to port in Port Fourchon.

On 01 June 2025 at 1827 UTC (1427 EDT) a Personal Locator Beacon (PLB) was detected at 44 21.1N 104 04.8W, in Sand Creek Crossing, WY. It was activated when 6 people on rented utility task vehicles became lost. attributes.description:
The Dutch Federal government has designated wind energy areas in the North Sea: Borssele, Hollandse Kust (south, north and west), IJmuiden Ver, North of the Wadden Islands, Nederwiek, Lagelander and Doordewind. The wind energy areas were designated (or reconfirmed) in the North Sea Programme 2022-2027. With a few exceptions, these areas lie outside the 12-mile zone, at least 22 kilometres from the coast. Only in these wind energy areas can plots for wind farms be issued under the Offshore Wind Energy Act. The moment a wind farm is under construction or in use, a safety zone is established around the area to be protected. Within that safety zone, ships are banned from entering, with some exceptions.

The spatial reference system is ETRS 1989 UTM Zone 31N

attributes.description:
The main purpose of Inland Fisheries Ireland???s NRSP (National Research Survey Programme) and Water Framework Directive (WFD) Rivers, Lakes, and Transitional and Coastal Water (TRAC) sampling programmes is to collect fish stock data relating to fish species composition, abundance and age structure in selected waterbodies nationally. These data are used to calculate Ecological Quality Ratings (EQR???s) for fish ecological status in each waterbody/site, a requirement for the EU Water Framework Directive. Data collected spans 2008 to most recent surveys. Multiple survey data by year are available for individual waterbodies and information from the most recent survey is displayed on the map viewer.

Where sp. or spp. denoted identification is to genus level only.

Common names of each fish species were taken from the Key to the Marine and Freshwater Fishes of Britain and Ireland ??? A guide to the identification of more than 370 species. By Peter S. Maitland and Douglas Herdson. Edited by Steve Coates. Published by the Environment Agency, UK. 2009

Programmes are part funded by the Department of Housing, Local Government & Heritage.

attributes.name: Water Framework Directive Transitional Waters Fish Ecological Status 2008 to Recent, Ireland
attributes.searchDescription: The main purpose of Inland Fisheries Ireland???s NRSP (National Research Survey Programme) and Water Framework Directive (WFD) Rivers, Lakes, and Transitional and Coastal Water (TRAC) sampling programmes is to collect fish stock data relating to fish species composition, abundance and age structure in selected waterbodies nationally. These data are used to calculate Ecological Quality Ratings (EQR???s) for fish ecological status in each waterbody/site, a requirement for the EU Water Framework Directive. Data collected spans 2008 to most recent surveys. Multiple survey data by year are available for individual waterbodies and information from the most recent survey is displayed on the map viewer. Where sp. or spp. denoted identification is to genus level only. Common names of each fish species were taken from the Key to the Marine and Freshwater Fishes of Britain and Ireland ??? A guide to the identification of more than 370 species. By Peter S. Maitland and Douglas Herdson. Edited by Steve Coates. Published by the Environment Agency, UK. 2009 Programmes are part funded by the Department of Housing, Local Government & Heritage. REST (JSON)

attributes.snippet: The main purpose of Inland Fisheries Ireland???s National Research Survey Programme (NRSP) and Water Framework Directive (WFD) Rivers, Lakes, and Transitional and Coastal Water (TRAC) sampling programmes is to collect fish stock data relating to fish species composition, abundance and age structure in selected waterbodies nationally. These data are used to calculate Ecological Quality Ratings (EQR???s) for fish ecological status in each waterbody/site, a requirement for the EU Water Framework Directive. Data collected spans 2008 to most recent surveys. Multiple survey data by year are available for individual waterbodies and information from the most recent survey is displayed on the map viewer.

attributes.description:
Inland Fisheries Ireland???s National Barriers Programme (NBP) developed a field survey to capture information on barrier location, type and associated images and structure dimensions. This form was used as a Level I assessment measure to find and locate barriers. The NBP has delivered a geo-referenced database fully integrated with EPA-WFD coding and instream structures can then be assessed by EPA sub-Catchment or waterbody codes. This is the framework with structures assessed during on-site visits are now populating.

This programme is funded by the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage (DHLGH).

attributes.description:
The City of Boulder Open Space and Mountain Parks (OSMP) Department funds scientific inquiry on OSMP lands on an annual cycle as part of its "Funded Research Program." This program started in 1995. The data file on the open data catalog has grant history going back to 2016. Earlier records are available, but are not collated and ready for release at this time; these records are, however, available upon request.

The Funded Research Program has four goals:

  1. Provide a mechanism for training scientists and land managers.
  2. Address short-term and long-term management needs.
  3. Solidify relationships with the research community.
  4. View Open Space as an integral part of the Front Range.

dataIdInfo.idAbs:
The City of Boulder Open Space and Mountain Parks (OSMP) Department funds scientific inquiry on OSMP lands on an annual cycle as part of its "Funded Research Program." This program started in 1995. The data file on the open data catalog has grant history going back to 2016. Earlier records are available, but are not collated and ready for release at this time; these records are, however, available upon request.

The Funded Research Program has four goals:

  1. Provide a mechanism for training scientists and land managers.
  2. Address short-term and long-term management needs.
  3. Solidify relationships with the research community.
  4. View Open Space as an integral part of the Front Range.

Each year, staff reviews incoming proposals for merit (proposal organization, management merit, intellectual merit, methods, personnel qualifications, schedule and resources) and decides which to fund. For more information, please see:??https://bouldercolorado.gov/osmp/funded-research-program

attributes.description:
A dataset of lichen records from combined list (includes SOWI, SWI, URI, LRI, BWI species see appendices below), and key additional species identified of relevance to Cairngorm region and identified by Dave Lamacraft and Oliver Moore:

- Anaptychia ciliaris subsp. Ciliaris VU

- Arthonia patellulata DD

- Bacidia circumspecta VU

- Bacidia igniarii VU

- Bacidia vermifera EN

- Biatora efflorescens NT

- Biatoridium delitescens VU

- Caloplaca ahtii DD

- Caloplaca flavorubescens EN

- Candelariella superdistans DD

- Catinaria neuschildii VU

- Collema occultatum

- Diplotomma pharcidium DD

- Lecania dubitans ??

- Lecania sambucina

- Lecanora populicola NT

- Lecidella flavosorediata ??

- Leptogium saturninum

- Rinodina laevigata DD

- Schaereria corticola DD

- Schismatomma graphidioides VU

 

Alistair Whyte Plantlife Scotland identified those above (highlighted in red) on the Scottish Biodiversity List (and added their threat status where known ??? several are endangered and data deficient). AW comments ???The SBL isn???t perfect, but it does have legal weight ??? public bodies (local authorities, agencies, national park authorities) must give ???due regard??? to these species. What that means has never been tested ??? the wording of the law has never enabled a case to be taken, and I would be wary about doing so here. But even highlighting the species and their SBL/ threat status could be powerful???.

 

In total 8815 records from 120 lichen species have been included in this analysis.

 

Data sources: Data was sourced from the NBN Atlas under a publicly accessible download, as well as from our internal hosting of the BLS database (as provided to us by the BLS in 2022). Majority of records within this dataset come from the British Lichen Society (BLS), however some also have been shared via the NBN from the National Trust for Scotland, the Highland Biological Recording Group and Northeast Scotland Biological Records Centre under a CC-BY and CC-BY-NC licenses.

 

Methodology: SOWI, SWI, URI, LRI, BWI lists, and additional species (above) were combined to create a master list. This list was used to interrogate the NBN Atlas and Plantlife internal copy of the BLS species database. All records for relevant species were collated. This large dataset was refined by removing all pre 2000 records and all 10km grid ref resolution records. Where higher resolution grid references were available in the free text fields these were moved to the spatial reference column to ensure the highest resolution grid reference was used to represent the plant location. Records were then mapped and those that fell outside of the Cairngorm National Park where removed.

 

Purpose of data capture: To identify key woodlands and areas of lichen richness within the Cairngorm National Park. This dataset has been used to further create a GIS layer showing 1km coincidence of lichen species richness.

 

Temporal Coverage: 2000-2023

 

Attribute field explanation: The list below is a subset of the information fields collected and submitted to the BLS for inclusion on their database. Where BLS coding is mentioned below, please see link : https://britishlichensociety.org.uk/sites/default/files/recording-mapping-downloads/BLS_General_v7.12_Jan2024.xlsx

 

- Attribute name: Description

- Taxon_Name: ???Scientific name

- Location: ???Location of observation

- Spatial_Reference: Ordnance Survey Grid reference

- X: ???Easting

- Y: Northing

- Lat: ???Latitude

- Long: Longitude

- Sample_Comment: Any additional comments on the sample by recorder (Obs_comment and Sample _comment are free text fields that add additional useful information to the record)

- Year: Year record observed

- Recorders: ???Name of person recording observation

- Obs_Comment: Any additional comments on the observation by recorder (Obs_comment and Sample _comment are free text fields that add additional useful information to the record)

- Substrate: Type of substrate species grows on (summarised using BLS coding system)

- Scale_Habitats__BLS: Next level of substrate classification (summarised using BLS coding system)

- Source: Where was the record accessed/downloaded from (e.g. NBN Atlas)

- Dataset_name: Name of dataset

- Rightsholder: Dataset owner

- Licence: Creative Commons licence records shared under

A dataset of lichen records from combined list (includes SOWI, SWI, URI, LRI, BWI species see appendices below), and key additional species identified of relevance to Cairngorm region and identified by Dave Lamacraft and Oliver Moore:

- Anaptychia ciliaris subsp. Ciliaris VU

- Arthonia patellulata DD

- Bacidia circumspecta VU

- Bacidia igniarii VU

- Bacidia vermifera EN

- Biatora efflorescens NT

- Biatoridium delitescens VU

- Caloplaca ahtii DD

- Caloplaca flavorubescens EN

- Candelariella superdistans DD

- Catinaria neuschildii VU

- Collema occultatum

- Diplotomma pharcidium DD

- Lecania dubitans ??

- Lecania sambucina

- Lecanora populicola NT

- Lecidella flavosorediata ??

- Leptogium saturninum

- Rinodina laevigata DD

- Schaereria corticola DD

- Schismatomma graphidioides VU

Alistair Whyte Plantlife Scotland identified those above (highlighted in red) on the Scottish Biodiversity List (and added their threat status where known ??? several are endangered and data deficient). AW comments ???The SBL isn???t perfect, but it does have legal weight ??? public bodies (local authorities, agencies, national park authorities) must give ???due regard??? to these species. What that means has never been tested ??? the wording of the law has never enabled a case to be taken, and I would be wary about doing so here. But even highlighting the species and their SBL/ threat status could be powerful???.

In total 8815 records from 120 lichen species have been included in this analysis.

Data sources: Data was sourced from the NBN Atlas under a publicly accessible download, as well as from our internal hosting of the BLS database (as provided to us by the BLS in 2022). Majority of records within this dataset come from the British Lichen Society (BLS), however some also have been shared via the NBN from the National Trust for Scotland, the Highland Biological Recording Group and Northeast Scotland Biological Records Centre under a CC-BY and CC-BY-NC licenses.

Methodology: SOWI, SWI, URI, LRI, BWI lists, and additional species (above) were combined to create a master list. This list was used to interrogate the NBN Atlas and Plantlife internal copy of the BLS species database. All records for relevant species were collated. This large dataset was refined by removing all pre 2000 records and all 10km grid ref resolution records. Where higher resolution grid references were available in the free text fields these were moved to the spatial reference column to ensure the highest resolution grid reference was used to represent the plant location. Records were then mapped and those that fell outside of the Cairngorm National Park where removed.

Purpose of data capture: To identify key woodlands and areas of lichen richness within the Cairngorm National Park. This dataset has been used to further create a GIS layer showing 1km coincidence of lichen species richness.

These data represent the 10 final study areas for the Aquaculture Opportunity Areas analysis for the Gulf of Alaska that were finalized in March 2024 based on the feedback received through the Request for Information (RFI).The final Alaska study areas included six areas located in Southeast Alaska, three in Southcentral, and one expanded area in Southwest Alaska. The study areas consisted of Alaska state waters within a 25 nautical mile radius of the communities of: Juneau, Sitka, Petersburg, Wrangell, Craig, Ketchikan, Seward, Valdez, and Cordova. In response to public and agency comments, the Kodiak Island study area was expanded to include areas in proximity to Old Harbor and Larsen Bay.

These data are published within the Alaska Digital Aquaculture Atlas. For more information, please reference the NOAA Inport metadata record.

attributes.description:
NCRMP biological monitoring (i.e., fish, corals, and benthic communities) uses a grid-based stratified random design that is optimized to efficiently sample for ecologically and economically important species. In the U.S. Caribbean, the NCRMP sample frame has two jurisdictions: (1) Puerto Rico, a single sampling domain or region; and (2) U.S. Virgin Islands, which consists of two separate sampling domains or regions: (a) St. Croix and (b) St. Thomas and St. John. Each region has a unique set of strata specific to the local protected or managed zones and benthic habitat.  The survey design ensures that survey sites for fish and corals are allocated by hard bottom habitat type, depth, and management zone, with sites distributed around the sampling region from nearshore to offshore to a maximum depth of 30 m.

This dataset contains the sampling sites for Puerto Rico for the 2025 survey mission.

The Reef Visual Census (RVC) is a stationary-point-count sampling protocol for reef fish. Field surveys used a one-stage design to sample within a selected subset of 50 m ?? 50 m grid cells. A two-diver RVC team surveyed all fish within adjacent 15-m diameter cylinders centered on each diver and extending vertically from the substrate to the sea surface. Within each cylinder, fish were identified to species and counted, and fork length was estimated to the nearest centimeter.

Corals and benthic communities were monitored using a Benthic Community Assessment survey and a Coral Demographics survey). The Benthic Community Assessment survey includes:

  1. benthic cover (%) estimates along a 15-m transect with a line point intercept method 
  2. presence/absence of Endangered Species Act (ESA)???listed coral species 
  3. abundance of key macroinvertebrates
  4. reef rugosity measurements within a 15 m ?? 2 m belt-transect area. 

At the same site, coral demographics were surveyed within a 10 m ?? 1 m belt-transect area. In Coral Demographics surveys, all live coral colonies ??? 4 cm were counted, identified to species, and measured to the nearest centimeter (length, width, height); estimates were made of the proportion per colony of any present mortality (recent or old), disease (present, slow, fast), and/or bleaching (total, partial, paling). Only live coral colonies were included in the survey; dead colonies with 100% mortality were not surveyed (e.g., colonies killed by coral disease). Juvenile corals (< 4 cm) were reported for species richness only and were not included in counts, size measurements, or estimates of condition.

Learn more at the project page.

Field surveys used a one-stage design to sample within a selected subset of 50 m ?? 50 m grid cells. A two-diver RVC team surveyed all fish within adjacent 15-m diameter cylinders centered on each diver and extending vertically from the substrate to the sea surface. Within each cylinder, fish were identified to species and counted, and fork length was estimated to the nearest centimeter. Corals and benthic communities were monitored using a Benthic Community Assessment survey and a Coral Demographics survey). The Benthic Community Assessment survey includes: benthic cover (%) estimates along a 15-m transect with a line point intercept method?? presence/absence of Endangered Species Act (ESA)???listed coral species?? abundance of key macroinvertebrates reef rugosity measurements within a 15 m ?? 2 m belt-transect area.?? At the same site, coral demographics were surveyed within a 10 m ?? 1 m belt-transect area. In Coral Demographics surveys, all live coral colonies ??? 4 cm were counted, identified to species, and measured to the nearest centimeter (length, width, height); estimates were made of the proportion per colony of any present mortality (recent or old), disease (present, slow, fast), and/or bleaching (total, partial, paling). Only live coral colonies were included in the survey; dead colonies with 100% mortality were not surveyed (e.g., colonies killed by coral disease). Juvenile corals (< 4 cm) were reported for species richness only and were not included in counts, size measurements, or estimates of condition. Learn more at the project page.

attributes.description:
NOAA conducted benthic habitat mapping of shallow-water coral reef areas off Puerto Rico to inventory the coral reefs and related bottom types. Before this project, a comprehensive inventory of the shallow-water reefs in these areas did not exist. Such an inventory is needed for successful coral reef ecosystem management. This represents the first U.S. coral reef area to be mapped under the purview of the U.S. Coral Reef Task Force.

NOAA acquired aerial photographs of the nearshore waters of Puerto Rico in 1999. These images, along with field sampling for validation, were used to create geographic information system (GIS) maps of the study area's coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangrove forests, and other important marine habitats. Mapped areas encompass the insular shelf between the shoreline and shelf edge, except where turbidity prevented visualization of the bottom. Products include GIS maps of benthic habitats, aerial photographs, an online benthic habitat atlas, along with a detailed methods manual for creating the benthic habitat maps.

NOAA mapped 21 distinct benthic habitat types within eight zones and added these data to a GIS using visual interpretation of orthorectified aerial photographs. NOAA mapped benthic features that covered an area of 1600 km2 in Puerto Rico, which included 721 km2 of submerged vegetation, 756 km2 of coral reef and colonized hardbottom, 49 m2 of unconsolidated sediment, and 73 km2 of mangroves.

Since 2002, these maps have been used for a wide range of applications, including coral reef monitoring, marine protected area design, fisheries assessments, and student projects.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands data page.

attributes.description:
The state of Wisconsin in 2014 proposed the creation of a national marine sanctuary with the goal of conserving a nationally significant collection of shipwrecks and other underwater cultural resources. These cultural resources are part of a broader interconnected lake ecosystem. This project collected and assessed key ecological information to map how lake resources are interconnected, and support monitoring, protection and management of ecological and cultural resources.

Data and assessments from this project supported the designation of the Wisconsin Shipwreck Coast National Marine Sanctuary. In addition, the maps and assessments will benefit a variety of other planners and policy makers such as the Wisconsin Historical Society, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and US Army Corps of Engineers.

This bathymetry raster, depth below lake level, was collected with a Kongsberg EM 2040C. The average standard deviation of depth was calculated in a 3x3 cell neighborhood. Image resolution is 1 meter.

Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

attributes.description:
The state of Wisconsin in 2014 proposed the creation of a national marine sanctuary with the goal of conserving a nationally significant collection of shipwrecks and other underwater cultural resources. These cultural resources are part of a broader interconnected lake ecosystem. This project collected and assessed key ecological information to map how lake resources are interconnected, and support monitoring, protection and management of ecological and cultural resources.

Data and assessments from this project supported the designation of the Wisconsin Shipwreck Coast National Marine Sanctuary. In addition, the maps and assessments will benefit a variety of other planners and policy makers such as the Wisconsin Historical Society, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and US Army Corps of Engineers.

NOAA collected new side-scan and multibeam mapping data off Manitowoc and Sheboygan, Wisconsin. These data were interpreted to map important lakebed habitats, substrates, invasive mussels and nuisance algae. These data are also being used to update nautical charts, and improve our understanding of lake habitats and underwater cultural resources.

The bathymetry was collected with LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) by the US Army Corps of Engineers. Average standard deviation of depth in a 3x3 cell neighborhood. Image resolution is 1 meter.

Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

These cultural resources are part of a broader interconnected lake ecosystem. This project collected and assessed key ecological information to map how lake resources are interconnected, and support monitoring, protection and management of ecological and cultural resources. Data and assessments from this project supported the designation of the Wisconsin Shipwreck Coast National Marine Sanctuary. In addition, the maps and assessments will benefit a variety of other planners and policy makers such as the Wisconsin Historical Society, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and US Army Corps of Engineers. NOAA collected new side-scan and multibeam mapping data off Manitowoc and Sheboygan, Wisconsin. These data were interpreted to map important lakebed habitats, substrates, invasive mussels and nuisance algae. These data are also being used to update nautical charts, and improve our understanding of lake habitats and underwater cultural resources. This bathymetry was collected with LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) by the US Army Corps of Engineers. The slope of slope measures the amount of change in bathymetric slope in the 3x3 cell neighborhood and is a measure of lakebed topographical curvature. Image resolution is 1 meter. Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

attributes.description:
Shallow-water and moderate-depth coral reef ecosystems in the surrounding waters of St. John are unique natural resources that must be preserved. The mosaic of habitats, including hard and soft corals, is home to a diversity of marine organisms that provide important ecosystem services to the community of St. John, including fishing, tourism, and shoreline protection.

Through the implementation of a multi-year Interagency Agreement, NOAA's Biogeography Branch mapped 53.4 km?? of shallow-water habitats around St. John and 90.2 km?? of moderate-depth habitats south of St. John for the Department of Interior, National Park Service, Inventory and Monitoring Program.

NCCOS developed benthic habitat maps for shallow areas (<30 m) around St. John and moderate-depth areas (30???60 m) south of St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands. These maps are helping local managers develop place-based strategies to address and remedy specific threats to coral reefs inside Virgin Islands National Park and the Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument.

This image represents a 2x2-meter resolution bathymetry surface of the moderate-depth portion of the NPS's Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument, south of St. John, US Virgin Islands. The depth values contained in this surface are in meters.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata from its data page.

attributes.description:
This map, created by NOAA's National Estuary Research Reserve, depicts the Kachemak Bay area watershed boundaries. Watershed boundaries were delineated from Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (IFSAR) on the south side of the bay and Lidar on the north side. The IFSAR data was collected 2010-2012 and the Lidar data was collected in 2008. The basin boundaries were derived from these datasets using the hydrologic modelling tools in ArcGIS followed by manual on-screen editing to correct obvious errors.

NOAA developed a benthic habitat map of Kachemak Bay using multibeam sonar data collected during hydrographic surveys conducted by the NOAA Ships Fairweather and Rainier. The area mapped is large and deep, approximately 71 kilometers long and 10 kilometers wide (229 square nautical miles), and approximately 170 meters at its deepest. To aid the development of the maps, NOAA used an extensive July 2016 field verification effort that visualized bottom habitats with underwater video.

Learn more at the project page and download the data from its accession page.

The seagrass map was generated by manual on-screen interpretation of the digital air photos, delineating habitat boundaries around seagrass features (e.g., areas with specific color and texture patterns). Also in 2005, an additional 81 intertidal seagrass sites were visited on foot during extreme low tides.

The area mapped is large and deep, approximately 71 kilometers long and 10 kilometers wide (229 square nautical miles), and approximately 170 meters at its deepest. attributes.description:
A baseline environmental characterization of the inner Kachemak Bay, Alaska was conducted using standardized National Status and Trends Bioeffects Program methods, the sediment quality triad approach based on sediment chemistry, sediment toxicity, and benthic invertebrate community structure. Three sites near the village of Port Graham were also sampled for comparison. Concentrations of over 120 organic and metallic contaminants were analyzed. Ambient toxicity was assessed using two bioassays. A detailed benthic community condition assessment was performed. Habitat parameters (e.g., depth, salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, sediment grain size, and organic carbon content) that influence species and contaminant distribution were also measured at each sampling site. Methods and results are reported in Hartwell et al. 2009, available for download. Results are also summarized in a NOAA Special Report (Hartwell et al. 2011), available for download as a pdf. The original data in downloadable tabular format can be accessed here.

NOAA developed benthic habitat maps for Kachemak Bay using multibeam sonar data collected during hydrographic surveys conducted by the NOAA Ships Fairweather and Rainier. The area mapped is large and deep, approximately 71 kilometers long and 10 kilometers wide (229 square nautical miles), and approximately 170 meters at its deepest. To aid the development of the maps, NOAA used an extensive July 2016 field verification effort that visualized bottom habitats with underwater video.

Learn more at the project page and download the data from its accession page.

attributes.description:
In recent years, flame retardant chemicals, known as polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDEs), have generated international concern over their widespread distribution in the environment, their potential to bioaccumulate in humans and wildlife, and concern for suspected adverse human health effects. NOAA???s Mussel Watch Program monitors the status and trends of chemical contaminants of U.S. coastal waters, measured in filter-feeding bivalves (oysters or mussels). The Mussel Watch Program conducted a study of PBDEs in bivalve tissues and sediments and published the results in a national-scale assessment (Kimbrough et al. 2009). This study features nine sample sites in Alaska, two of which are in or near Kachemak Bay (sites CIHS Homer Spit and CINK Nanwalek) with mussel (Mytilis sp.) as the sampled species. Levels of PBDEs in mussel tissues at these sites are considered ???medium??? because they are above zero. Trends are not reported, since there was only one sample year (2005) for these sites. This summary report (Kimbrough et al. 2009) is available for download

NOAA developed benthic habitat maps for Kachemak Bay using multibeam sonar data collected during hydrographic surveys conducted by the NOAA Ships Fairweather and Rainier. The area mapped is large and deep, approximately 71 kilometers long and 10 kilometers wide (229 square nautical miles), and approximately 170 meters at its deepest. To aid the development of the maps, NOAA used an extensive July 2016 field verification effort that visualized bottom habitats with underwater video.

attributes.description:
NOAA???s Mussel Watch Program monitors the status and trends of chemical contaminants of U.S. coastal waters, measured in filter-feeding bivalves (oysters or mussels). This national assessment (Kimbrough et al. 2008) reports results for eight metals (Arsenic, Cadmium, Copper, Mercury, Nickel, Lead, Tin, and Zinc) and six classes of organic contaminants (Butyltins, Chlordanes, DDTs, Dieldrins, PAHs, and PCBs). Results are generally reported in parts per million (ppm) dry weight for metals, and parts per billion (ppb) dry weight for organic contaminants. This study features five sample sites in Alaska, one of which (site CIHS, Cook Inlet ??? Homer Spit) is in Kachemak Bay, with mussel (Mytilis sp.) as the sampled species. Sampling was done in 2005, and compared with previous years to discern trends for each contaminant (increasing, decreasing, or no trend). An aggregate index is calculated for both metals and organic contaminants, reported as Metals_status, Metals_trend, Organic_status, and Organic_trend. Levels for most contaminants at site CIHS are ranked as ???low???, with no discernable trends. Arsenic (As) occurs naturally in some glacial-origin sediments of Alaska and is the only contaminant ranked as ???medium??? in this study. This summary report (Kimbrough et al. 2008) is available for download.

The area mapped is large and deep, approximately 71 kilometers long and 10 kilometers wide (229 square nautical miles), and approximately 170 meters at its deepest. To aid the development of the maps, NOAA used an extensive July 2016 field verification effort that visualized bottom habitats with underwater video.

attributes.description:
This image represents a 1x1-meter resolution backscatter mosaic of Jobos Bay, Puerto Rico (in NAD83 UTM 19 North). The backscatter values are in relative 8-bit (0 ??? 255) numbers, since the SoNAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) sensor was not calibrated. Different benthic habitat types were delineated and classified from this backscatter image.

NOAA studied the water contaminant levels in the bay and the coral reef ecosystems just outside to develop a baseline environmental assessment of water quality and living marine resources of Jobos Bay. The bay is home to important marine habitats but is surrounded by farms which can adversely affect water quality in the bay through runoff of pesticides and fertilizers. The baseline assessment will be used to assess effectiveness of agricultural best management practices in the watershed.

Jobos Bay is Puerto Rico???s second largest estuary and home of the Jobos Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve. The Bay has a variety of important marine habitats including mangroves, salt marshes, and seagrass beds.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata from its data page.

server.description:
This image represents a 1x1 meter resolution backscatter mosaic of Jobos Bay, Puerto Rico (in NAD83 UTM 19 North). The backscatter values are in relative 8-bit (0 ??? 255) numbers, since the SoNAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) sensor was not calibrated. Different benthic habitat types were delineated and classified from this backscatter image.

NOAA studied the water contaminant levels in the bay and the coral reef ecosystems just outside to develop a baseline environmental assessment of water quality and living marine resources of Jobos Bay. The bay is home to important marine habitats but is surrounded by farms which can adversely affect water quality in the bay through runoff of pesticides and fertilizers. The baseline assessment will be used to assess effectiveness of agricultural best management practices in the watershed.

Jobos Bay is Puerto Rico???s second largest estuary and home of the Jobos Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve. The Bay has a variety of important marine habitats including mangroves, salt marshes, and seagrass beds.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata from its data page.

attributes.description:
This image represents a 50x50 meter principal component (PC) surface for areas inside Buck Island Reef National Monument (BIRNM). This PC surface describes seafloor's topography and structure, which is important information when characterizing the seafloor. It was ultimately derived from the depth surfaces collected by USGS (in 11 to 4,670 m of water) using a SeaBeam 2112 multibeam echosounder (MBES). Several metrics were derived from these depth surfaces, including: (1) mean depth, (2) standard deviation of depth, (3) curvature, (4) plan curvature, (5) profile curvature, (6) rugosity, (7) slope, and (8) slope of slope images. These images were stacked and transformed into their first three principal components using Principal Components Analysis. This transformation removed information that was redundant across the different images. This PC image (along with backscatter) was used to develop a new benthic habitat map for BIRNM in 1,000 to 1,830 meters of water.

This project began in April 2010 and was completed in January 2012. NCCOS developed benthic habitat maps for the BIRNM, north of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The bathymetry (depth) data was used to update nautical charts in the area and the related habitat maps are being used by local managers to plan research projects and site-related infrastructure inside the monument, such as placing receivers for the acoustic tracking of fish and sea turtles.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the Buck Island Reef National Monument, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands data page.

attributes.description:
This dataset shows the variation in the predicted probability of occurrence for live coral reef (all species) for select areas offshore of Saipan, CNMI. Variation is described as coefficient of variation (CoV). CoV is unitless and is the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean for each pixel. It was calculated by creating 100 separate models, and then calculating the mean and standard deviation of probability of occurrence in each pixel across the models.

The project was based on high resolution WorldView II satellite imagery collected post-Typhoon Soudelor, use of ground validation data from throughout the lagoon, modelling the probability of occurrence of individual substrate and cover types, combining model layers into a classified benthic map, and thematic as well as spatial accuracy-assessment using independent field data.

This work was conducted in close partnership with CNMI's Bureau of Environmental Quality and NOAA's Pacific Island Fisheries Science Center CNMI Field Office.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the NCEI Accession page.

attributes.description:
NOAA developed a map of benthic habitat types, including live coral cover present off northeast Puerto Rico and Culebra Island, a region selected by local managers as a priority area for habitat mapping. The map covers 744 km2 of shallow-water habitats at a high spatial resolution (the smallest habitat features mapped are 10??10 meters) and includes 250 km of shoreline for the region's 210 islands and rock outcrops. This includes the shallow habitats inside the current boundaries of the Northeast Natural Reserves, as well as surrounding areas. The habitat map, generated using a combination of semi-automated classification and visual interpretation techniques of remote sensing imagery (WV-2 satellite imagery collected 2011-2013, hydrographic data collected 1900-2012 and aerial photos collected 2007-2010) and underwater videos (2013-2014), represents the first digital map that describes nearly 100% of the seafloor in the study area.

This image represents a 1-meter resolution backscatter mosaic of the bathymetry of a reef shelf/bank and the steep slopes and canyons of the NE Reserve, offshore of Fajardo, Puerto Rico. NOAA's NOS/NCCOS/CCMA Biogeography Team, in collaboration with NOAA vessel Nancy Foster and territory, federal, and private sector partners, acquired multibeam bathymetry data in the Northeast Reserve during 2012 and 2013. Data was acquired with a moon pool mounted Reson 7125 multibeam echosounder (400 kHz). Data is in UTM zone 20 north, datum NAD83. The backscatter component of the bathymetry data were geometrically and radiometrically corrected using .HSX and .7k file pairs that were converted to GSF format in Hypack 2012, then processed in Fledermaus Geocoder Toolbox 7.3.3c. Acoustic backscatter mosaics are an important piece of information when characterizing surficial seafloor features and delineating benthic habitats. The project was conducted to meet IHO Order 1 and 2 accuracy standards, dependent on the project area and depth. All users should individually evaluate the suitability of this data according to their own needs and standards.

Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

documentInfo.Comments: The primary purpose of this database was to provide researchers, managers, and the public with an accurate and highly detailed benthic habitat map of Northeast Puerto Rico (NEPR). Habitat maps provide a spatially explicit representation of benthic structure and biological cover. The spatial products developed for this project will: (1) inform local managers as to the current distribution of resources, (2) provide a point of comparison for past and future mapping efforts, (3) help locate sensitive marine communities, and (4) guide monitoring efforts and prioritize management actions.

Data was acquired with a moon pool mounted Reson 7125 multibeam echosounder (400 kHz). Data is in UTM zone 20 north, datum NAD83. The backscatter component of the bathymetry data were geometrically and radiometrically corrected using .HSX and .7k file pairs that were converted to GSF format in Hypack 2012, then processed in Fledermaus Geocoder Toolbox 7.3.3c. Acoustic backscatter mosaics are an important piece of information when characterizing surficial seafloor features and delineating benthic habitats. The project was conducted to meet IHO Order 1 and 2 accuracy standards, dependant on the project area and depth. All users should individually evaluate the suitability of this data according to their own needs and standards.

Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

attributes.description:
This GeoTiff is a model from the principal component analysis (PCA) of the seafloor of Northeast Puerto Rico that contains the shallow water area (0-30m deep) of the Northeast Ecological Reserve: including the waters off of Fajardo and Luqillo, to the Former Roosevelt Roads Navy Base, the Vieques Sound, La Cordillera Reserve, the Luis Pena Reserve, and the waters around Culebra Island. The PCA was created using Envi 5.1 imagery analysis by combining the morphometric derivatives of the bathymetry and statistically analyzing the variance and spatial complexity of the seafloor to create the model. The source bathymetry model was produced by merging soundings from several different sources, including high resolution coastal LiDAR, NOAA multibeam bathymetry, and historical lead line soundings. The PCA provided the biogeography with the data to delineate the different benthic habitats of the NER.

Learn more at the project page, which contains links to download the datasets.

attributes.description:
This dataset consists of accuracy assessment and ground validation sites used to construct the benthic habitat maps of Guam. The quality of the habitat information derived from remotely sensed data is determined by the quantitative process of accuracy assessment and ground validation. The purpose of accuracy assessment is to identify and quantify errors in the maps by comparing the attributes of the map versus reference data at various sites. Selected sites were visited in the field for typological validation.

The ground validation sites were visited in the field for typological validation. This validation included: 1) areas in the imagery with confusing or difficult to interpret signatures, 2) transects across many representative habitat types occurring in different depths and water conditions, 3) a survey of the zones, and 4) confirmation of preliminary habitat delineations if a first draft was produced. Individual sites were visually evaluated by snorkeling and free diving or directly from the boat in shallow, clear water. Habitat transitions were evaluated by swimming transects across habitat types to further guide placement of polygon boundaries. Habitat type(s), zone, approximate depth, position (GPS), image number, and other descriptive information were recorded at each site. Field data for each site was then compiled into a text table with a latitude/longitude field to allow overlay of the field information on the mosaic and habitat polygons.

The accuracy assessment sites are a statistically robust data set composed of random field habitat observations were collected within the test areas to assess the accuracy of the mapped product. These areas were chosen based on input from the local marine biologists and coral reef managers. These groups provided advice on the location of the most diverse benthic communities and also areas of particular importance based on management strategies and marine protected areas.

The data is part of the Benthic Habitat Mapping in American Samoa, Guam, and Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands project, which mapped the coral reef habitats of the islands by visual interpretation and manual delineation of IKONOS satellite imagery. The project produced a georeferenced, digital atlas of benthic habitat maps for the shallow-water (< 30m) coral ecosystem habitats that support a variety of management applications, including informing resource management decisions, ensuring safe navigation, supporting coastal communities, sustaining coastal habitats, and mitigating coastal hazards.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the Guam data page.

documentInfo.Comments:
This project is a cooperative effort between the National Ocean Service, National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science, Center for Coastal Monitoring and Assessment, the University of Hawaii, BAE Systems Spectral Solutions and Analytical Laboratories of Hawaii, LLC. The goal of the work was to map the coral reef habitats of American Samoa, Guam and the Common Wealth of the Northern Mariana Islands by visual interpretation and manual delineation of IKONOS satellite imagery. A two tiered habitat classification system was tested and implemented in this work. It integrates geomorphologic reef structure and biological cover into a single scheme and subsets each into detail. It also includes thirteen zones. Benthic features were mapped that covered an area of 104 square kilometers of which 32.9 were unconsolidated sediment and 71.6 were coral reef and hard bottom. Of the coral reef and hard bottom class, 35.6% is colonized by greater than 10% coral cover.

For more information, see http://coastalscience.noaa.gov/projects/detail?key=261

attributes.description:
NOAA conducted benthic habitat mapping of shallow-water coral reef areas off Puerto Rico to inventory the coral reefs and related bottom types. Before this project, a comprehensive inventory of the shallow-water reefs in these areas did not exist. Such an inventory is needed for successful coral reef ecosystem management. This represents the first U.S. coral reef area to be mapped under the purview of the U.S. Coral Reef Task Force.

This benthic mapping activity was conducted to inventory the reef ecosystem and associated bottom types for Puerto Rico. Prior to this project, a comprehensive inventory of the shallow water ecosystems in these areas did not exist. Such an inventory is required for successful management. To meet this need, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Biogeography Branch, in consultation with many local and federal partners conducted a GIS based mapping effort in the region. This represents the first US coral reef area to be mapped under the purview of the US Coral Reef Task Force. The classification scheme defines benthic communities on the basis of two attributes: large geographic "zones" which are composed of smaller "habitats".

Since 2002, these maps have been used for a wide range of applications, including coral reef monitoring, marine protected area design, fisheries assessments, and student projects.

Thematic accuracy of the Puerto Rico habitat maps was evaluated for the three most general habitat categories: unconsolidated sediment, submerged vegetation, and coral reef/hard bottom. Data recorded at each site included habitat type, depth, and other descriptive information. Depth was determined using a hand-held depth sounder. Habitat type(s) were recorded within an approximately 5- to 7-meter radius around each pre-selected site.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands data page.

attributes.description:
This dataset shows the average predicted probability of occurrence (%) for Live Coral (Encrusting) for select areas offshore of Saipan, CNMI.

Average probabilities were calculated by creating 100 separate models, and then averaging the predicted probabilities in each pixel across the models. Lower probabilities (closer to 0%) indicate a habitat type is less likely to be present. Higher probabilities (closer to 100%) indicate a habitat type is more likely to be present.

The project was based on high resolution WorldView II satellite imagery collected post-Typhoon Soudelor, use of ground validation data from throughout the lagoon, modelling the probability of occurrence of individual substrate and cover types, combining model layers into a classified benthic map, and thematic as well as spatial accuracy-assessment using independent field data.

This work was conducted in close partnership with CNMI's Bureau of Environmental Quality and NOAA's Pacific Island Fisheries Science Center CNMI Field Office.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the NCEI Accession page.

attributes.description:
This dataset consists of accuracy assessment and ground validation sites used to construct the benthic habitat maps of American Samoa.

The accuracy assessment sites were generated to assess the accuracy of the individual maps created from IKONOS satellite imagery. GPS field observations were used to establish the thematic accuracy of this thematic product. 651 benthic habitat characterizations were completed for this work.

The ground validation sites were selected to specifically investigate habitat types and gradients of spectral signatures. All areas where uncertainty existed on the part of the photo interpreter during habitat delineation were investigated in the field. 347 field positions were occupied and habitat characterization conducted for ground validation during this work.

The data is part of the Benthic Habitat Mapping in American Samoa, Guam, and Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands project, which mapped the coral reef habitats of the islands by visual interpretation and manual delineation of IKONOS satellite imagery. The project produced a georeferenced, digital atlas of benthic habitat maps for the shallow-water (< 30m) coral ecosystem habitats that support a variety of management applications, including informing resource management decisions, ensuring safe navigation, supporting coastal communities, sustaining coastal habitats, and mitigating coastal hazards.

Learn more at the project page and download data and metadata at the American Samoa Data page.

documentInfo.Comments: This project is a cooperative effort between the National Ocean Service/ National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science/Marine Spatial Ecology, the University of Hawaii, BAE Systems Spectral Solutions and Analytical Laboratories of Hawaii, LLC. The goal of the work was to map the coral reef habitats of American Samoa, Guam and the Common Wealth of the Northern Mariana Islands by visual interpretation and manual delineation of IKONOS satellite imagery. A two tiered habitat classification system was tested and implemented in this work. It integrates geomorphologic reef structure and biological cover into a single scheme and subsets each into detail. It also includes thirteen zones. Benthic features were mapped that covered an area of 71.5 square kilometers of which 10.56 were unconsolidated sediment and 60.94 were coral reef and hard bottom. Of the coral reef and hard bottom class, 62.8% is colonized by greater than 10% coral cover.For more information, see https://coastalscience.noaa.gov/project/benthic-habitat-mapping-american-samoa-guam-commonwealth-northern-mariana-islands/

attributes.description:
This dataset shows the variation in the predicted probability of occurrence for Algae (Halimeda spp.) for select areas offshore of Saipan, CNMI.

Variation is described as coefficient of variation (CoV). CoV is unitless and is the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean for each pixel. It was calculated by creating 100 separate models, and then calculating the mean and standard deviation of probability of occurrence in each pixel across the models.

The project was based on high resolution WorldView II satellite imagery collected post-Typhoon Soudelor, use of ground validation data from throughout the lagoon, modelling the probability of occurrence of individual substrate and cover types, combining model layers into a classified benthic map, and thematic as well as spatial accuracy-assessment using independent field data.
